kept.heading: THE HARMS OF SHORT-FORM VIDEO ON THE BRAIN ARE STARTING TO SHOW (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Heavy short-form video use may impair attention and memory. A meta-analysis of about 70 studies found stronger links to cognitive problems than mental health issues, with compulsive use predicting worse outcomes. Other research links more phone time to poorer working memory and uncontrolled short-form use to weaker episodic memory. Memory and imagination share neural circuitry, so these effects could also make it harder to envision and plan for the future.

Title: Zuckerberg says the science isn’t settled. But the harms of short-form video on the brain are starting to show

URL Source: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/sep/14/zuckerberg-short-form-video-cognitive-harm

Published Time: 2026-09-14T11:00:57.000Z

Markdown Content:
A few years ago, when I’d just started graduate work, I was waiting with a grandmother finishing a questionnaire I’d handed her about her 19-year-old granddaughter who was in the testing room next door. They were participating in a study that used brain imaging to look at adolescent development. The older woman had a soft southern accent and a warm laugh.

“What’s funny?” I asked.

“Cellphone use,” she said, gesturing at a question about how much time her granddaughter spent on her device. “When is she not on it? And my younger granddaughter, she just turned 18 – I mean, I think she’d die if you took the phone away from her.”

I told her that’s what I studied – “well,” I said. “Mostly social media.”

“Social media!” She shook her head. “Sometimes I think that’s the worst thing that ever happened to us.”

In the years since, that sense of broad, far-reaching harm has worked its way from our collective consciousness into [thousands](https://time.com/article/2026/08/11/tech-social-media-addiction-tiktok-meta-snap-google-lawsuits/) of high-profile lawsuits currently making their way through US courts. Last week, [yet another began](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/new-mexico-facebook-meta-florida-cambridge-b3047434.html) in New Mexico, [focused on user data and the Cambridge Analytica scandal](https://www.krqe.com/news/new-mexico/new-mexico-takes-facebook-back-to-court-over-data-privacy-violations/). In October, teenagers in Los Angeles will [argue that Meta, YouTube and Snap](https://www.beasleyallen.com/publication/jere-beasley-report-september-2026/) caused serious mental health issues.

The most high-profile suits have focused on adolescent mental health, child sexual exploitation and, to a lesser extent, data privacy.

But in the years I’ve been researching how digital media is changing us, I’ve been increasingly concerned with how little we know about its cognitive effects, particularly those of short-form video, the format that now dominates every social media platform.

The vague sense that we are being cognitively hollowed out, dulled and diminished by our latest technology is captured in the term “[brain rot](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-brain-rot-is-2024s-word-of-the-year/)”, recognized by the makers of the Oxford English Dictionary as the 2024 word of the year. And the more researchers look at it, the more it seems to describe distinct cognitive changes that are now being borne out by science.

The literature is still limited, but the most recent meta-analysis, published in Psychological Bulletin, [examined the roughly 70 quantitative studies](https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2026-89350-001.html) focused on the mental health and cognitive effects of short-form video. The majority of this research comes from China, where platforms are heavily regulated. Still the authors found an association with negative cognitive changes – stronger, in fact, than the association with poorer mental health.

The strongest relationships were with attention and impulse control. But relatively few studies looked at anything else, such as memory, decision-making, language or reasoning. In that analysis, the available research on memory amounted to a single study.

Whether individuals described their use as compulsive – or something they couldn’t control – predicted the worst cognitive outcomes.

Mark Zuckerberg and other social media [executives](https://apnews.com/article/instagram-social-media-addiction-trial-mosseri-los-angeles-a49f64e21682e8bc1b98fbdf3d061579) have [repeatedly](https://www.apa.org/news/press/op-eds/zuckerberg-social-media-harmful)[argued](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YuIc4mq7zMU) that current science doesn’t back up public concern. And it’s true that active social media use – connecting with friends and family, sharing updates, writing and creating content – [can be psychologically and cognitively](http://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7801842/) beneficial.

The trouble is, tech companies have increasingly ignored the preferences of their users and promoted passive engagement, pushing the zombie-making infinite scroll and time-dissolving short-video feed – a digital format that seems almost universally damaging.

In my own research, I’ve found surprising relationships between memory and both cellphone use and short-form video. These early findings call for replication, but they held even after accounting for depression and anxiety.

The more time young adults spent on their phones, the worse they performed on a test of working memory, the system that holds information in mind while you’re using it. What you rely on to follow an argument or carry out a plan.

And in study participants who described their short-form video use as out of control, episodic memory was measurably weaker. This form of memory might be thought of as the internal record of your own life – the ability to travel back and revisit various moments. It is how we develop our sense of self in relationship to the world over time.

I’ve been dogged by the idea that, due to my own digital media habits, I might be moving through my days with a befogged sense of what I just did. What I should do next.

Even more alarming is the possibility that we are becoming less and less self-aware and creative in our own internal lives. Memory and imagination run on the same circuitry. In a [2007 study](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0610561104), patients with damage to the hippocampus, the brain’s memory hub, struggled to construct imagined scenes. Remembering the past and picturing a reality you haven’t lived [appear to be the same act](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0028393206004131), run in opposite directions. If we are degrading the one, we might be degrading the other, damaging our ability to envision and enact a new future.

Perhaps these cognitive relationships feed on themselves as a sort of cyclone, driving diminished capacity that in turn results in more helpless digital media consumption. Perhaps collective cognitive changes could have large sociological or political implications.

The head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said in a state trial in California last February that he [doesn’t think Meta products are “clinically addictive](https://ca.rollingstone.com/instagram-head-adam-mosseri-testifies-says-problematic-use-is-not-clinical-addiction/)”. And on semantics, he’s right. The only behavioral addiction the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [currently recognizes is gambling](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4458066/).

But clinical addiction doesn’t have to be the mechanism behind what we observe as problematic use. With all my concerns about the cognitive effects of short-form video, I’ve still been unable to quit [Meta](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/meta) platforms. After many rounds of locking myself out, I always come back for the flickers of old Facebook, where I might stay connected to people and communities I care about. Where I can see a friend launch a brilliant new mosaics venture, or my mother organize events for her town’s bike community, thousands of miles away.

A peace negotiator and member of a working group I convened at the [Santa Fe Institute](https://www.santafe.edu/) described social media platforms as holding our most important relationships hostage. To access them, we wade daily through brain-rotting media we would otherwise choose to avoid.

The price we pay for connection is our own minds.

In its most recent legal settlement, Meta agreed to pay $17bn and make design modifications to better protect 13- to 17-year-olds: a two-hour daily cap across Facebook and Instagram; a lockout between midnight and 6am, with notifications silenced from 10pm; hidden “like” counts; a ban on cosmetic-surgery filters; and the option to return to an un-optimized-for-your-attention news feed.

The settlement doesn’t include rationales or any admissions of culpability. But implicit in the changes is the idea that short-form video, lack of choice, and passive, mindless consumption are the main culprits. Direct messages with personal contacts and long-form content are excluded – the things users both want and that we know are relatively safe.

Though the settlement is only geared towards protecting a subset of adolescents, what research we have suggests social media’s cognitive risks affect teenagers and adults equally. We all have grounds for wanting greater control over our digital environment.

It may be just a matter of time before cognitive research can do for social media what decades of epidemiology did for lead in the 1960s, 70s and 80s: allow concerned citizens to push for corporate changes that make the world [safer for everyone](https://www.greatamericaninsurancegroup.com/content-hub/environmental-insider/understanding-the-evolution-of-lead-regulations).

Science and litigation will continue to lag behind the relentless pace of big tech. Knowing this, perhaps the safest way to approach the digital world, where we now spend most of our time, is to listen to our own minds and bodies. The science is telling us that teens – and their grandmothers – knew intuitively that something was wrong, even if research will take years to prove exactly what it was.

*   Caty Enders is a journalist and researcher exploring our relationship to technology. She writes the newsletter [Standing in the Current](https://standinginthecurrent.substack.com/)

Title: Has mainstream culture disappeared? New YouTube trends research says no

URL Source: https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/

Published Time: 2026-09-10T13:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Black bold text reading "Culture & Trends Report" set against a white background, bordered on the bottom and left edges by colorful, glossy, swirling marble spheres.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/images/YouTube-Mainstream-Report-Cove.max-100x3000.format-webp.webp)

## New research from YouTube and NRG explores how creators, memes, and digital lore break through to wider audiences.

* * *

Sep 10, 2026[[read-time]] minute read

### Listen to article

[Audio 3](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/media/tts_audio_86180_umbriel_2026_09_10_17_30_29.mp3)

What defines mainstream culture in an era where everyone’s feed looks completely different? According to YouTube’s latest Culture & Trends Report, **_In Search of Mainstream_**, our cultural landscape is more fragmented than ever, but the mainstream hasn't disappeared—its meaning has just shifted.

To learn more about the modern mainstream, the YouTube Culture & Trends team partnered with NRG to review prevailing themes in recent research, analyze entertainment, media, and video trends from around the world, and run surveys asking thousands of people about their interests and attitudes toward culture. Respondents were active online, age 14–44. Below, we explore the core findings of the report and what they reveal about the future of shared culture.

## **Has mainstream culture actually disappeared?**

Not at all, but its meaning has shifted. Audiences have access to more content, communities, and creators than at any other point in history. The result is a culture that is more personalized and less synchronous.

Yet shared moments still break through. **63% of 14- to 29-year-olds agree that being into the same things as other people makes them feel part of something bigger**. [1](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/#footnote-1) The difference is that, increasingly, culture begins online, gaining momentum within digital communities before reaching wider audiences.

![Image 2: A Venn diagram titled "There's More Than One Way to Matter" illustrates how visibility, comprehension, and participation overlap to define modern culture. Overlapping sections categorize culture into "Known" (visibility and comprehension), "Popular" (visibility and participation), "Niche" (comprehension and participation), and "Mainstream" at the center of all three.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/original_images/3-square.gif)

## **How do we measure what is "mainstream" today?**

It has become increasingly difficult to understand when something has broken through as older signals have become less relevant in our increasingly digitally mediated culture. Through our research, we have identified three signals that shape the modern version of mainstream and can help us measure the cultural breakthrough of phenomena.

**Visibility:** A measure of repeated exposure and awareness across platforms and conversations. At its peak, a topic becomes so ubiquitous that it feels impossible to ignore.

**Comprehension:** A measure of shared understanding across diverse audiences. At its peak, a topic requires little to no explanation, transforming into a cultural shorthand, an important quality that separates the mainstream from the merely popular.

**Participation:** A measure of cultural momentum as a result of active engagement with a topic. As it reaches its peak, it reflects widespread participatory behaviors—spanning commenting, sharing, creating, remixing, and purchasing.

69%

of respondents have watched content from a community they would consider niche

## **Are digital creators and memes really on par with traditional celebrities?**

When survey respondents were asked what lots of people seem to be into nowadays, digital entities like **YouTube creators (77%)** and **memes (78%)** were perceived to be as widely known as **Hollywood celebrities (79%)** and the **Super Bowl (83%)**. [2](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/#footnote-2)

71% have watched videos unpacking stories within a specific fandom or community, while 69% have watched content from a community they would consider niche. [3](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/#footnote-3) This is a signal that audiences are actively exploring and helping shape what becomes important next, and that the average person's cultural diet may now consist of more niche ideas than mainstream ones.

## **How does internet lore turn into a Hollywood blockbuster?**

YouTube has created new entry points into culture. A prime example is **"The Backrooms,"** which originated as a single creepy photo before fan communities expanded the concept through fan art, theories, stories, and forums.

Director Kane Parsons (@KanePixels) adapted the lore into a found-footage YouTube series, with the first short drawing over 90 million views. [4](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/#footnote-4) That online momentum culminated in an A24 theatrical adaptation that opened to **$118 million globally**, setting a studio record and making Parsons the youngest director to ever top the global box office. What was once a niche concept had grown into a mainstream phenomenon, culminating in a fan-driven theatrical event.

73%

agree YouTube is the best place to deeply explore their personal interests.

## **Why do younger fans care so much when their favorite creators succeed?**

For Gen X, “selling out” was the worst thing an artist could do. Millennial hipsters inherited a version of that mindset too, with discovery and niche taste becoming forms of cultural currency. Today, younger audiences see success differently.

*   **63% of fans** agree: _"I feel successful when the person or thing I'm a fan of experiences success."_[5](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/#footnote-5)
*   **60% of fans** feel proud because they believe they actively helped build that success.

Because audiences participate in creating, sharing, and amplifying what they love, cultural breakthroughs feel increasingly like shared achievements.

## **What role does YouTube play in cultural validation?**

In an era of limitless content, visibility is everywhere, but comprehension is scarce. Audiences turn to YouTube not just to find what exists, but to understand why it matters:

*   **65%** agree that something feels more real or legitimate when they see it show up on YouTube. [6](https://blog.youtube/culture-and-trends/youtube-culture-trends-modern-mainstream-research/#footnote-6)
*   **73%** agree YouTube is the best place to deeply explore their personal interests.
*   **72%** say they stay interested in things long after discovery because of YouTube.

But every website you open now has this widget:

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uET4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40c88ddf-33af-4ac1-a028-65ef4bf5c5bb_3032x1280.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uET4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40c88ddf-33af-4ac1-a028-65ef4bf5c5bb_3032x1280.png)

[Port](https://port.io/)’s website has the same Slack widget…

**But it says it’s a human:**

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xmAP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3bb7c42-46a4-4b01-aec6-1b5b3121fb32_1378x597.png)](https://port.io/)

Smart! 🧠

That’s the biggest trend in tech right now: **everybody wants a human**.

Even if your bot is smarter and faster than a person, people don’t want to be the guinea pigs who test it. A human is more reliable right now, and a human has all the privileges, like issuing a refund or opening the admin panel.

Your competitors replaced people with bots wherever they could, so a human who answers is rare now. That’s AI fatigue working for you.

So here are 3 ways to put humans back into your marketing ↓

Port’s widget is a Slack connector: your message goes into their Slack.

[Legit Security](https://www.legitsecurity.com/) does the same with a “Chat over Slack” button, right next to “Book Demo”:

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hVCU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa76fdb77-615e-45a5-87f1-be589b51156d_1207x254.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hVCU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa76fdb77-615e-45a5-87f1-be589b51156d_1207x254.png)

[Gartner asked](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-07-09-gartner-survey-finds-64-percent-of-customers-would-prefer-that-companies-didnt-use-ai-for-customer-service) thousands of customers about AI in customer service, and 53% said they’d consider switching to a competitor if they found out a company was going to use it.

**Do this:**

*   💻 Change your chat’s opening message to “Real person here! I’m [Name], write to me and I’ll answer”, and replace the robot icon with your photo. Then answer it yourself.

*   🌌 Add an offline message so the promise holds while you sleep: “It’s [Name], I’m offline. Leave your email and a person replies within one business day”. If you don’t have a widget at all → put your name and face next to the support email instead.

[Aerie](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2026/03/30/aerie-doubles-down-on-its-no-ai-pledge-in-its-latest-campaign) pledged to never use AI-generated people in its ads:

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2xUC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a6491ea-e27a-4b8d-b514-2151d3aa7a5e_1653x928.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2xUC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a6491ea-e27a-4b8d-b514-2151d3aa7a5e_1653x928.png)

Aerie’s pledge

It became the brand’s [most-liked](https://www.instagram.com/reels/DWWTYWTEfBj/) Instagram post with 40,000+ likes, and that quarter’s sales grew 23%. (Correlation, I know. I’d still take it.)

Among people under 30, [66% react negatively](https://news.gallup.com/poll/713222/americans-aren-sold-businesses-using-advertising.aspx) to businesses using AI in ads. Yup, the AI-friendly generation is allergic to AI ads!

**Do this:**

*   ✏️ Write a post like Aerie’s - along the lines of “we will never use AI for [the thing your customers care most about]”.

*   👱🏻‍♀️ Sign the product: “Made by [Name] and [Name]”, with photos, in the footer or on the About page.

*   🌈 Put a sentence on your pricing page (or your support page): “Every support reply here is written by a person, at 2 AM too”.

At a recent conference, **we built a branded “No-AI Zone” near the entrance**, with free coffee, board games, a postcard-writing station, and a working mailbox. Most booths inside were selling AI.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!L8QB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbda63ac5-e621-4e42-8c33-a107e1922575_1280x1606.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!L8QB!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbda63ac5-e621-4e42-8c33-a107e1922575_1280x1606.webp)

Wiz’s no-AI zone

I've been collecting examples since I wrote about [proof it’s human](https://www.marketingideas.com/p/how-to-find-customers-when-90-of) last November, and my favorite is [Ramp](https://www.marketingideas.com/p/5-viral-marketing-moves-that-will?utm_source=publication-search): they put Kevin from The Office in a glass office in Manhattan, doing expense reports by hand for 7 hours, and the clips passed 85M views.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_shA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa50311b2-0d38-4532-aac4-9ea3e227ab3e_2872x2154.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_shA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa50311b2-0d38-4532-aac4-9ea3e227ab3e_2872x2154.png)

Ramp’s stunt

Ramp’s own [explanation](https://www.linkinbio.news/p/ramp-b2b-marketing-playbook) to this stunt: “We wanted to show something real in an AI world”. _*chef’s kiss*_

A few more from the past year:

*   **[Cursor](https://www.aol.com/articles/went-cursors-york-caf-saw-101401630.html)** rents a café for a day and puts its engineers in name tags so users can come meet them. The NYC slots had a waitlist.

*   **[Thursday](https://www.globaldatinginsights.com/featured/thursday-shutters-dating-app-to-shift-focus-on-real-world-events/)**, the dating app, shut down its own app and became an in-person events company, now in about 150 cities.

*   **[Pinterest](https://newsroom.pinterest.com/news/coachella-2026-phone-free/)** ran a phone-free space at Coachella: phones locked in pouches at the door, and a printed guide instead of QR codes.

*   **[Hinge](https://hinge.co/newsroom/one-more-hour-2026)** has given $2.3M to running clubs and book clubs (yes, a dating app paying people to get off the app).

Anthropic’s version was the “thinking” hat, and I waited [2 hours](https://www.marketingideas.com/p/what-to-do-if-your-marketing-sucks) in line for mine.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vize!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc07c152b-e6dd-41b9-91c4-ca41070fc4c8_2270x1690.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vize!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc07c152b-e6dd-41b9-91c4-ca41070fc4c8_2270x1690.png)

café cursor

**Do this:**

*   ⚙️ The cheapest version is office hours in a café, in a city where your customers already are (or the day before a conference you’re attending anyway). Post from your own account: “I’m at [café] on [day], 9 to 11. Come by and I’ll fix your homepage in person, coffee’s on me”. About $40 in coffee, and Cursor had a waitlist for theirs.

*   🍔 Host a dinner for 8-10 customers, phones in a basket at the door.

*   🎪 If you have a booth this year → set up a folding table where someone does the task your product automates, by hand, in front of everyone, under a sign that says “This is what [product] replaces”.

Have an amazing week ✌️

Tom

kept.heading: THE NEW RULES OF GROWTH (WEBINAR)
kept.blurb: High-growth marketing teams are changing how they hire and allocate resources as growth demands rise. On September 17, Krithika Shankarraman of Thrive Capital and Christy Roach of AirOps will share how they secure resources, measure newer channels like AI Search, and get more leverage from smaller teams as growth accelerates.

Title: The New Rules of Growth | AirOps Webinar | AirOps.com

URL Source: https://www.airops.com/events/webinar-the-new-rules-of-growth

Markdown Content:
Marketing teams are being asked to deliver more with higher pipeline targets, changing buyer behavior, and limited resources, but the teams that are growing fastest are operating under a very different set of conditions.

Join Krithika Shankarraman (Marketing at Thrive Capital) and Christy Roach (CMO of AirOps) as they break down the results from the _Marketing Leaders Reality Index_ and how high-growth teams are changing the way they hire, prioritize, report, measure success, and work with the rest of the business.

Krithika and Christy are both veterans of high growth culture, having been early employees at companies like Stripe, OpenAI, Asana, Gusto, and Airtable. In this live conversation, they’ll unpack what sets high-growth teams apart, what’s different about how they operate, and what marketing leaders can apply to their own operations to accelerate growth and secure more resourcing for their teams.

Go deeper into operating principles that set high-growth teams apart from the rest.

## **What you'll learn:**

*   What growing marketing teams are doing differently across hiring, resourcing, prioritization, and operating models
*   How to make the case for additional budget and headcount when pipeline targets are rising faster than resources
*   Where marketing leaders should push back on executives and boards, and how to connect investment decisions to business growth
*   How high-growth teams are changing the way they measure success, report performance, and build confidence in new channels like AI Search
*   What smaller, more senior teams are doing to increase leverage without simply producing more
*   How to operate differently once you have the resources to grow, from team design and workflows to accountability and decision-making

## **Speakers**

[Krithika Shankarraman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/krithix/) was the first marketing hire at Stripe and at OpenAI, helping build both marketing functions from the ground up. An engineer turned marketer, she now leads marketing at Thrive Capital and helps founders across the portfolio with all things marketing.

[Christy Roach](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christy-roach/) is the CMO at AirOps, where she helps brands drive growth via AI search. Before AirOps, she was CMO at AssemblyAI and held marketing leadership roles at high-growth technology companies including Airtable, Asana, and Gusto.

Join Rachel Duffy, Head of Community at The Times and Sunday Times, and founder of the Young Journalists Network, in this conversation with Rob Fawkes from Standing on Giants on what winning on Reddit actually looks like for a major media brand, and what any company can take from it.

**What we'll cover:**

*   A jargon-buster intro on Reddit basics: karma, moderators, subreddit culture

*   How Rachel built a Reddit strategy from scratch 

*   The wins in brand visibility, traffic and community trust, and how moderator relationships actually work day to day

Title: Does Retail Media Add Value?

URL Source: https://www.practicalecommerce.com/does-retail-media-add-value

Published Time: 2026-09-13T13:31:24+00:00

Markdown Content:
Retail media is advertising published by retailers. Amazon Sponsored Products is the best-known example.

Retail media creates value for advertisers when it generates profitable new demand, but it can just as easily shift margin to the underlying ecommerce site publishing the ads.

The retail media market is substantial and growing.

A 2025 Journal of Retailing [paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jretai.2025.08.005) estimated 2024 global retail media spending at more than $140 billion, including $54 billion in the United States. More recently, [eMarketer forecasts](https://www.emarketer.com/content/retail-media-ad-spending-forecast-trends-h2-2025) U.S. retail media ad spend at $69.33 billion in 2026, a 17.9% increase from 2025.

Distribution of U.S. Retail Media Spend, 2025

Pie chart with 0 slices.

Top retailer-publisher channels

PRACTICAL ECOMMERCE | Source: Statista

End of interactive chart.

### Using Retail Media

Ecommerce companies can participate on either side of the retail media market.

A merchant selling through Amazon, Walmart, or other marketplaces can buy ads to convert more shoppers.

The same merchant can also sell and publish ads on its own site and email list.

For the advertiser, retail media can be useful because the message appears close to the purchase decision. A shopper searching for “waterproof hiking boots” shows a strong purchase intent.

### Value Creation

Imagine a brand that spends $1,000 on retail media and generates $5,000 in sales it would not otherwise have received. If those sales produce $1,500 in contribution margin before advertising, the campaign generated $500 in net benefit.

That is [value creation.](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/google-criteo-deal-unlocks-retail-media)

The economics look different when the sale would have happened anyway.

Imagine a marketplace where a seller historically ranked well organically. The marketplace adds more sponsored placements, competitors bid for them, and the seller must spend $5 on advertising to maintain a $50 sale it used to get without that expense.

*   The marketplace earns $5 more.
*   The seller earns $5 less.
*   The shopper still purchases the same product.

Retail media has generated revenue for the marketplace, but not for the advertiser.

This possibility is more than theoretical. The Journal of Retailing report noted concerns that retail media can erode advertisers’ margins when the attributed sales are not incremental or new.

![Image 1: Screenshot of hiking shoes in a sponsored products ad](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/091126-sponsored-product-570x321.jpg)

Retail media in the form of sponsored placements can turn an ecommerce storefront into an advertising channel, such as this example for hiking shoes.

### Lowers Profit

Moreover, retail media can erode the margins of merchants publishing the ads

Consider a retailer with a category page generating $100,000 in monthly merchandise sales and $30,000 in gross profit.

A supplier agrees to pay $3,000 per month for a prominent advertising placement, seemingly elevating margins to $33,000.

But suppose the sponsored placement displaces the merchant’s own conversions. Gross profit falls from $30,000 to $28,000.

The retailer-publisher collected $3,000 in media revenue but gained only $1,000 overall.

Even worse, if gross profit from product sales falls to $26,000, the $3,000 from retail media _lowered_ overall margin by $1,000.

Advertising revenue increased. Business performance declined.

That risk extends beyond a single product. Too many sponsored products or irrelevant recommendations could make a store harder to shop, weaken customer trust, or reduce conversions over time.

For marketplace advertisers, [return on ad spend](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/Using-ROAS-to-Measure-Advertising-Results) cannot alone justify the investment. An advertiser generating $8 in sales for every $1 ad may have received those conversions anyway.

The more useful measure is whether the advertising changed the outcome.

To estimate the effect, large advertisers use randomized experiments, marketing mix models, geo-testing, and similar methods. Smaller companies can assess new-customer sales, organic performance, and periods with and without campaigns.

### Incremental Value

Thus retail media is not inherently a win or loss.

If it creates profitable new demand for advertisers, it’s a win. If it adds cost to conversions advertisers would have received anyway, it’s a loss.

For retailer-publishers, it adds value only if it produces a higher net margin.

That [distinction](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/retail-medias-performance-dilemma) matters for both sides of retail media.

Title: Are you doing marketing… or building software?

URL Source: https://www.growth-memo.com/p/are-you-doing-marketing-or-building

Published Time: 2026-09-14T10:03:27+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lYw3!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3341e6b5-2b60-417d-b845-96f5effd4973_2400x1600.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lYw3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3341e6b5-2b60-417d-b845-96f5effd4973_2400x1600.png)

This Memo was sent to 29,183 subscribers. Welcome to +80 new readers! Sign up for free to get new insights every week, or sign up for Premium to get exclusive tools and frameworks that make you more effective.

The most valuable 30 minutes in marketing right now are the 30 minutes you spend thinking _before_ you start building any AI automation.

Last week’s Memo made the case that[AI does not delete marketing work, it moves it](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/the-ai-hours-nobody-on-your-marketing), and that the bill often gets paid out of the least attributable work your team does. Prompting, checking, editing, fixing, and maintaining are all real work hours, and they come from somewhere.

The question now is what to do about it.

All of the work your marketing team does with AI comes from 3 places:

1.   AI-powered software/tooling from a vendor

2.   Expert customization and implementation from a consultant who has already built it

3.   Time from your team to build it in-house

Amanda and I work separate client rosters, but the same pattern is showing up in both: Teams aren’t sorting their AI work hours in a targeted manner. Instead, they’re going straight to attempting to automate as much as they can in-house.

Automating in-house is smart. But skipping the sorting step (which takes 30 minutes or less), is an expensive mistake. Thankfully, it’s an easy fix.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8__B!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F479a5843-f669-43c1-9468-3279cee4198d_1638x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8__B!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F479a5843-f669-43c1-9468-3279cee4198d_1638x2048.png)

Rank tracking, citation monitoring, brand mention tracking, crawl diagnostics, and content scoring are not unique to you.

Despite $30-40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI, [MIT’s review of enterprise AI projects](https://mlq.ai/media/quarterly_decks/v0.1_State_of_AI_in_Business_2025_Report.pdf) reveals that 95% of organizations are getting zero return. From the report:

> _Strategic partnerships achieved a significantly higher share of successful deployments than internal development efforts. While we observed far more BUILD initiatives than BUY initiatives in our sample, with many more organizations exploring internal development… success rates favored external partnerships. Though we lack precise data on total initiative volumes, the pattern suggests that internal development efforts have substantially lower success rates despite being more commonly attempted._

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yr2X!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f205ebf-8bb7-4a1e-a03a-436be11371ec_2048x1790.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yr2X!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f205ebf-8bb7-4a1e-a03a-436be11371ec_2048x1790.png)

The missing 1% from the chart above is MIT’s third structure, _hybrid build-buy,_ where an internal team co-develops with a vendor; the report had too little data to quantify it.

The report found the main reason projects fail is tools that do not learn or plug into how people already work. Making a tool fit is one of the most expensive parts, and a software vendor who’s already done that for 4,000 customers has done work you really don’t need to repeat.

When you’re deciding whether or not to build vs buy, you’re evaluating the software platform fee vs. what an hour of your team’s time really costs, multiplied by the hours it takes to build and maintain the internal version. (Plus the hidden hours nobody is counting: brainstorming, meeting, testing, reiterating, retesting.)

To be fair: I recognize this argument dangerously sounds like one of the Growth Memo sponsors could’ve written it. (They didn’t.) It’s simply wise resource planning, and it takes work off your team long-term.

Buy the tool when the problem is common. When you do, your team also gets 2 things you cannot build for yourself: the vendor maintains the software, and somebody on the other end fixes it when it breaks.

**Defending your marketing team’s build decision to a skeptical CFO requires real numbers**. The Growth Memo [AI Automation Work Router](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/ai-automation-work-router) prices vendor license fees against what your team’s or consultant’s hours actually cost, corrects your estimate against the research, and reveals the maintenance hours that usually appear on nobody’s budget. Premium subscribers also get the Router’s decision tree as slides, so you can run the meeting on 1 shared picture (instead of 6 competing opinions).

Some workflows really are yours, like who signs off on the work before it’s shipped, how your data is structured, when reporting goes out, how you gather SME input for content, or adding branded CTAs from a pre-approved copy bank.

This is where your team can accidentally burn the most hours, because “nobody else can build this” gets heard as “we have to build this ourselves.”

The workflow is yours, yes, but someone who has built 65 of these for 20 different teams already knows which steps usually break, which ones need input from your individual contributors, which ones are worth automating, and which ones look automatable but aren’t.

Your team is finding all of that out for the first time, on the clock.

Here’s the test: **If the hours you are about to spend produce knowledge you will not need weekly, contract out the knowledge instead.**

We both individually sell consulting, so you can read that with the appropriate squint. The point stands true _without_ hiring either of us: Buying the know-how looks like a template someone already validated, a contractor for 4 weeks, a consulting hour with a peer who has shipped the same thing, or a resource library built by people who made the mistakes first.

What it avoids: Your team discovering the failure modes one at a time.

This Memo’s sponsor, AirOps, is taking the same resource-allocation question one level up: Once you decide what to buy, build, or hand to an expert, how should the team allocate the time and budget left?

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fUDG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F79e7b45e-5c09-4d48-88f8-59c5b3308126_1080x1080.png)](https://www.airops.com/events/webinar-the-new-rules-of-growth?utm_source=growth-memo&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=NA_en_Webinar_The-New-Rules-of-Growth_Q3-2026&utm_content=newsletter)

That’s the focus of _The New Rules of Growth_, a free conversation on Thursday, September 17 at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET. Krithika Shankarraman, the first marketing hire at Stripe and OpenAI who now leads marketing at Thrive Capital, joins AirOps CMO Christy Roach.

They’ll unpack findings from the Marketing Leaders Reality Index and discuss how fast-growing teams design their organizations, prioritize initiatives, allocate resources, report performance, and make the case for additional budget and headcount.

[Reserve your spot](https://www.airops.com/events/webinar-the-new-rules-of-growth?utm_source=growth-memo&utm_medium=paid-newsletter&utm_campaign=NA_en_Webinar_The-New-Rules-of-Growth_Q3-2026&utm_content=newsletter)

Only [13% of marketers](https://technologychecker.io/blog/ai-in-marketing-statistics-use-cases) fully trust AI output without a human reading it. While that often gets treated as a model maturity problem or AI adoption hurdle, it’s actually a staffing requirement.

I (Kevin) ran into a situation where I was trusting my own AI workflow output slightly too much. When I took a pause and looked at it through a refreshed critical lens, I found a pile of wrong things to correct and reoriented the workflow accordingly.

And I (Amanda) had a case where my client generated a report from GSC data and sent it to me for feedback before bringing it into their weekly meeting. The model read a spike in a specific set of queries as proof of rising AI visibility and was glaringly wrong; the report was nearly on its way to the head of marketing to inform crucial decisions. We caught it. Now every report gets a human read before it leaves.

The [State of CRM Data Report 2026](https://www.validity.com/resource-center/state-of-crm-data-report-2026/) found the following:

> _“Nearly 78% of C-suite and 92% of SVP/VPs respondents say they have acted on an AI recommendation they later suspected was wrong because of bad underlying data, compared with 41% of individual contributors.”_

So if the majority of inputs and outputs need review (and perhaps, even an intervention before an output lands in the CMO’s inbox), someone who knows the subject has to do the reviewing, **which means the tool did not remove the skill required to do the work.** Judging the work is the harder, less-replicable of the tasks.

The rule that comes out of both experiences: Never buy or build a tool for a job nobody on your team can verify accuracy for by hand. You won’t be able to tell when it breaks (and it will break confidently).

**Premium is $150/year.**The [AI Automation Work Router](https://members.growth-memo.com/resources/ai-automation-work-router) alone saves you the afternoon your team would spend debating about whether to build something a vendor already sells (bonus: the auto-generated meeting notes and slide version and saves you building the deck to explain the answer). They’re in the [premium resource library](https://library.growth-memo.com/premium), along with 45+ other tools, checklists, and stakeholder decks.

With that in mind, this section is the actual method to use when making the build vs. buy decision, and it’s the part teams can get wrong even if they sort the work correctly.

Where failure can creep in at the start: A team names a slow process, decides AI should run the whole thing, and starts building something that does 15 steps. 6 weeks later, they have in-house software with no real tests, no documentation, and one person who understands how to maintain it with maybe 2-3 people who know how to run it.

A _**job**_ is a bundle of steps with judgment distributed across all of them.

A _**step**_ has one input, one output, and a check that takes seconds.

[Part 1](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/the-ai-hours-nobody-on-your-marketing) made the point that every workflow you build becomes a small permanent job to maintain. That’s true. And it’s an argument for making the job small, not for skipping it.

A one-step swap has one input to validate, one output to eyeball, and one thing to fix when the model version changes, while your 15-step workflow has 15 places to break and no fast way to find out which one did.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!t0-G!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0efe7761-74e4-4eca-9733-21b080d57ff8_1620x754.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!t0-G!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0efe7761-74e4-4eca-9733-21b080d57ff8_1620x754.png)

Take the process your team wants to automate and write out what actually happens, in order. Then mark each step with 3 things:

1.   **The input:** What arrives, and where does it come from? A step whose input is “context from the last meeting” is not a step yet.

2.   **The output:** What leaves, in what format? If the answer is a paragraph of judgment, keep looking.

3.   **The check:** How does a person confirm the output is right, and how long does that take? The verification check is real work and takes real time; plan for it.

The step you want to automate is the one that is slow, repetitive, tightly defined, and checkable at a glance.

Here’s a Growth Memo example: I built the new Growth Premium members’ area to include any of the _new_ tools and skills we’re building, but I automated it to go back into the archives to locate each prior premium asset and build an easy-to-find page around it.

1.   **The input:** Historical Growth Memo posts, specifically gated sections

2.   **The output:** A simple, easily searchable page with a link to the asset and notes on how to use it, along with an area for members to leave feedback/comments for admin

3.   **The check:** A 5 minute review before setting the page live

Usually an automatable step looks like a “small transformation:” raw data into a formatted table, a transcript into tagged quotes or first draft, internal linking across content clusters, a spreadsheet into a brief skeleton, a GSC export into a list of pages to refresh.

I (Kevin) would say there are 3 types of jobs that people do that people try to automate:

1.   Reporting (easy to automate)

2.   Synthesizing (hard to automate)

3.   Deciding (semi-hard to automate)

Anything requiring experienced taste, or any automated task where being wrong could be invisible for 3 months (like automating regular updates to meta titles and descriptions, checked quarterly), usually is an indicator that careful consideration is needed.

Use these guidelines to disqualify an in-house build:

*   Nobody on the team can do it “by hand,” so nobody can grade or verify the output.

*   The check takes longer than doing the work (unless you’re producing long-form drafts, which naturally take time for review).

*   The input changes often, which means you can’t easily maintain the workflow.

*   It touches a system you do not control, where an update on a Tuesday could break the workflow on a Wednesday.

Experimenting earns its keep. But your common problems should go to a vendor; there’s a reason why they exist. Problems that are yours and that your team deeply understands can go to someone who has built something similar before.

And the stuff that’s left… that’s the actual in-house AI workflow experimentation. Give it an owner, a kill date, and a sentence describing what winning looks like.

Everything else is software development, and, well, you didn’t hire your marketing team to write software.

Title: Research: 3 in 4 Americans use phones while watching TV

URL Source: https://www.advanced-television.com/2026/09/14/research-3-in-4-americans-use-phones-while-watching-tv/

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://atv-adsrv.com/images/43ec45a2fc710bfd4c049932604ca638.jpg)](https://atv-adsrv.com/ads/www/delivery/cl.php?bannerid=810&zoneid=17&source=%7Bobfs%3A%7D&sig=f9a1760f3bf04527c4903c6a420d8363f63f7cb1aa3b7e3d2934c647512d315d&oadest=https%3A%2F%2Fbridgetech.tv%2Fproducts%2Fvbcserver%2F)

The TV may still be the biggest screen in the room, but it no longer commands the room. Omdia consumer research unveiled by María Rúa Aguete, Global Head of Media & Entertainment at Omdia, at IBC reveals how smartphones are competing with TVs for attention in living rooms.

Around three in four US TV viewers regularly use other media on their smartphones while watching television, fragmenting attention between the big screen and the mobile screen. And this is no longer predominantly a young audience behaviour.

[![Image 2](https://atv-adsrv.com/images/3922d909127f9c69c56fa3f2832c94cf.jpg)](https://atv-adsrv.com/ads/www/delivery/cl.php?bannerid=742&zoneid=18&source=%7Bobfs%3A%7D&sig=0f68c0f0f7bf0c00fcc3121a41089f9ba0b57a33c833a3035a8e0c3087ab28ff&oadest=https%3A%2F%2Fjoom.ag%2FRDDd)

Omdia’s research shows some of the strongest growth in simultaneous media use is now among older viewers. Among US adults aged 55–64, the proportion using other media while watching TV has risen from 42 per cent in 2023 to 56 per cent in 2026. Among those aged 45–54, it has increased from 62 per cent to 73 per cent.

The findings point to a fundamental change in the competitive landscape for television. TV is no longer simply competing with another programme, streaming service or channel. It is increasingly competing with the smartphone in the viewer’s hand, and particularly with short-form video.

“We don’t have a content problem. We have an attention problem,” said Rúa Aguete, Global Head of Media & Entertainment at Omdia. “Three in four Americans are using their phones while watching TV, and increasingly what they are doing is watching more video. The battle is no longer simply TV versus mobile. Both screens are on. The question is: which one has your attention?”

Short-form and vertical video are becoming increasingly important in that battle. Audiences have become accustomed to scrolling through highly personalised, instantly accessible video on their phones, creating a very different competitive environment for traditional television and streaming services.

For broadcasters, streaming platforms, advertisers and content owners, Omdia believes this creates both a challenge and an opportunity. The industry must increasingly think about TV and mobile together, rather than treating them as separate viewing environments.

Rúa Aguete added: “The future isn’t TV versus mobile. It’s TV and mobile. The companies that understand how audiences move between those screens, and how to capture attention on both, will be best positioned to win.”

The findings were presented at IBC 2026 in Amsterdam as part of Omdia’s latest research into changing video consumption, the attention economy and the rapid growth of short-form and vertical video.

[![Image 3](https://atv-adsrv.com/images/63e59bc5378f2d540eaa69b4e9a0ad7a.jpg)](https://atv-adsrv.com/ads/www/delivery/cl.php?bannerid=607&zoneid=19&source=%7Bobfs%3A%7D&sig=26f8f43d5af731d8dc66013dda9f77f92b1c5c15f4b24b1e46e13fbb58d382d7&oadest=https%3A%2F%2Fadvanced-television.com%2Fcategory%2Fmagazines-euromedia%2F)

September 14, 2026

A handful of new job postings tie thought leadership to revenue instead of article counts. It is a small trend with a clear signal: owned media is turning into an operating function.

[![Image 13: Google Icon](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69d5f4156c1e2de2879d2837/6a13c9bfa24746699092f7de_Google_Favicon_2025.svg%201.avif) Add State of Brand on Google](https://ter.li/6uh2y55q)

Read a certain kind of job posting closely and you can watch a category change shape.

When Workato made its [first dedicated thought leadership hire](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/workato-thought-leadership-content-pipeline), the telling detail was not the title but where the role sat. Alex Lamascus, now Senior Director of Thought Leadership, moved the function closer to the sales floor than the comms team and started measuring it on win rates, deal velocity, and average sales price rather than reach and downloads. "The primary value of content is not only gaining attention," he told State of Brand. "It's building business infrastructure." That is a different job than the one most content teams are hired to do, and a growing number of companies are now hiring for it: newsroom-style editorial leaders held accountable to revenue.

For most of the last decade, content lived in an odd spot inside B2B marketing. Everyone agreed it was necessary and nobody could price it, so it got measured in outputs (posts shipped, words filed, downloads captured) mostly because the line to actual money was too hard to draw. These new hires bet that the line can be drawn now, and that whoever owns it should be senior, editorial, and carrying a number like anyone else with a budget.

## The reporting line is the story

What matters in the Workato example is not that a company hired for thought leadership. Companies have done that for years. It is that the job answers to pipeline rather than to article counts, and that one change lifts owned media out of the cost-center framing that has always held it back and drops it into the same accountability as demand gen and sales.

That framing has been a documented trap for a while. The [B2B CMO leadership research](https://www.b2bcmoproject.com/research) makes the point that the metrics marketers reach for to prove their worth, the MQLs and the cost-per-lead figures, are the same metrics that get them treated as a tactical function and a cost center. Report in the language of marketing outputs and you get read as marketing overhead. A thought leadership hire tied to pipeline refuses that framing from the first day. The scorecard is not how much shipped. It is what the point of view moved.

There is solid evidence that it moves a lot. The [2025 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report](https://www.edelman.com/expertise/Business-Marketing/2025-b2b-thought-leadership-report), the most authoritative recurring study in the space, found that 75% of decision-makers say a piece of thought leadership prompted them to look into a product or service they had not previously considered. For anyone thinking about competitive displacement, the sharper number is this: [70% of C-suite executives say thought leadership has led them to reconsider a current vendor.](https://www.ragan.com/edelman-and-linkedin-report-thought-leadership/) It is one of the few content types that pulls customers toward you and loosens a competitor's hold at the same time.

## You are publishing for the buyer you never meet

Part of why this function is professionalizing now is that the buying group got more crowded, and the people who tip a decision are the hardest to reach any other way.

The 2025 Edelman and LinkedIn work centers on what it calls hidden buyers, the internal influencers who shape a decision without ever surfacing in a sales conversation. [71% of them say they have little or no interaction with sales teams.](https://www.edelman.com/insights/hidden-buyer-b2b) A rep cannot get to them, because they never take the meeting. But [63% spend more than an hour a week reading thought leadership](https://www.edelman.com/insights/hidden-buyer-b2b), and 81% say strong thought leadership helps them see challenges or opportunities they had not recognized. The one channel that reaches the decision-shaper you can't book is exactly what a good editorial operation produces, which is a specific reason to fund it as a capability rather than an occasional campaign.

It also explains why the new roles sit so high. Reaching a skeptical, senior, hidden audience that reads an hour a week in your category is not junior work. It takes editorial judgment about which position is worth staking, a quality bar high enough to clear one that most thought leadership fails (in the Edelman-LinkedIn data, decision-makers rate the overall quality of what they read as middling, with only a sliver calling it very good), and the standing to kill the safe, on-message copy that gets ignored. That is an editor's job, which is presumably why the postings are starting to read like one.

## From projects to a standing operation

Underneath the hires is a move from thought leadership as a run of projects to thought leadership as a permanent operation with an owner, a standard, and a number.

[Ascend2 and TopRank's research](https://ascend2.com/new-research-answer-engine-the-state-of-b2b-thought-leadership-in-2026/) draws the line plainly: a one-time report buys attention, while a recurring research program builds ownership of a topic. Publish on a real cadence and you become the default authority in your space, the name the market, and increasingly the AI systems, reach for by habit. Default status like that is not something a team sprints to at quarter's end. It compounds, which means it needs an owner whose job is to keep it compounding rather than a rotating set of contributors squeezing it between other work.

Hiring an editorial leader and pointing them at pipeline is how a company turns that into an operation. It treats the point of view as an asset the business intends to build and hold, not a campaign it runs and shelves. The signal in these first roles is that a few companies have decided owning their narrative is a function with a seat and a scorecard, not something marketing does when it finds the time.

Expect the rest of the market to follow, because the alternative is to keep producing content no senior buyer remembers while a competitor becomes the name the category reaches for. The companies writing these job descriptions now are betting the revenue-tied newsroom is about to become standard equipment. Given where buyer attention has gone, that is not a reckless bet.

Title: Gen Z romanticised the library into relevance again

URL Source: https://www.firstpost.com/lifestyle/gen-z-romanticised-the-library-into-relevance-again-14042932.html

Published Time: 2026-09-03T18:30:43+05:30

Markdown Content:
From aesthetic morning routines to customized library card flexes, viral content is driving a physical resurgence that could save public libraries.

![Image 1: Gen Z romanticised the library into relevance again](https://images.firstpost.com/uploads/2026/09/Untitled-design-2026-09-03T182924.332-2026-09-6d614cc2ed372f82a933c4392118ee75-1200x675.jpg?im=Resize,width=720,aspect=fit,type=normal)

On platforms like TikTok and Instagram, creators routinely post "come to the library with me" videos, show off customised library cards, and film quiet study sessions under grand vaulted ceilings.

The virality of these videos highlights a curious plot twist in modern digital culture. Content creation—the very thing usually blamed for destroying our attention spans—is driving a massive, physical revival of public library visits. Against all odds, quiet civic infrastructure has become the internet’s most wholesome flexing opportunity.

Rather than treating libraries merely as places to check out books, these videos frame them as sanctuary spaces. Far from being simple internet fluff, this digital romanticisation provides public libraries with free, high-impact publicity. Beyond traditional bookshelves, institutions like [Finland’s Oodi Library](https://www.firstpost.com/lifestyle/in-finlands-oodi-library-you-can-record-podcasts-borrow-tools-and-even-sew-your-clothes-14027550.html) or various municipal branches across London showcase an evolving suite of civic tools, offering everything from podcast recording studios, sewing machines, and 3D printers to Pilates classes and tech workshops.

When creators vlog their visits, online enthusiasm translates into tangible foot traffic, providing local councils with the exact patronage numbers needed to justify funding and keep these public spaces open.

## Why younger people are flocking to libraries

Data from the American Library Association reveals that young adults use public libraries at higher rates than older generations, with 67 per cent of Gen Z reporting library visits in recent years. This movement is largely fueled by a desperate search for the "third place"—a public environment outside of home and work that does not require commercial participation. In an era where stepping outside almost guarantees spending money, libraries remain one of the few places where anyone can study, work remotely, or hang out without the social tax of buying an oat milk latte.

![Image 2: lifestyle](https://images.firstpost.com/dlxczavtqcctuei/news18/static/images/fp/revamp_v1/lifestyle.svg)More from Lifestyle

Research indicates that 85 per cent of Gen Z actively seek physical spaces to unwind, and those who visit libraries consistently report lower metrics of loneliness compared to non-visitors. Interestingly, over half of the young adults who do not even identify as active readers still visit their local library regularly to use the workspaces, access free technology, or attend community events.

## Reading is cool again

The surge in library content coincides with a broader aesthetic movement where physical media has regained massive cultural currency. Despite being born into a world of screens, Gen Z reads and buys roughly twice as many print books per month as e-books or audiobooks, treating physical paper as a deliberate form of digital detox.

Alongside the library visits, reading itself has picked up a new kind of [high-fashion accessory](https://www.firstpost.com/lifestyle/the-coolest-accessory-of-2026-a-book-under-your-arm-13987581.html). Being seen with a book has become its own small status symbol, enough that "book stylists" now curate literature for high-profile clients to carry when stepping out in front of paparazzi. It's a strange endpoint for an activity that used to be the default way to look like you were doing nothing, but it says something about where reading sits culturally right now that it needed styling in the first place.

By framing public [libraries](https://www.firstpost.com/lifestyle/dua-lipa-opens-library-of-banned-books-inside-one-of-the-worlds-most-beautiful-bookshops-14027526.html) not as dusty relics, but as vibrant, free community hubs, younger generations are ensuring these spaces remain active, funded, and cherished for years to come.

kept.heading: DON'T USE QUESTIONS IN YOUR TITLES (1 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Use statement-based headlines instead of questions to increase engagement with marketing content. A Stanford study found that question titles generated 71.6% fewer comments and 12.6% fewer clicks across experiments and analyses of more than 22,000 news articles, 3 million academic articles, and 53,000 Reddit posts. Questions may perform worse because they signal uncertainty and provide less immediate information to readers. Test statement formats such as “X compared to Y” against question-based titles, then check that title changes don't hurt SEO.

#### 📈**Recommendation**

Use statements for your headlines and titles (e.g. “When you need to optimize for AEO”), not questions (e.g. “Do you need to optimize for AEO?”).

kept.article_text:
Title: Stop Trying to Go Viral. You Need the Right 100 People to Know Who You Are First.

URL Source: https://themarketinglabuk.substack.com/p/stop-trying-to-go-viral-you-need

Published Time: 2026-09-15T06:50:38+00:00

Markdown Content:
i think we’ve become slightly obsessed with the wrong number. followers. 10k followers. 50k followers. 100k followers. everyone celebrates the milestones, and i get it, i’ve done it too 👀 but here’s the thing i’ve learned from building The Marketing Lab and watching 100s of marketers build personal brands: 10,000 people seeing you once is **nowhere near****as valuable**as 100 of the right people seeing you repeatedly.

this is one of the **biggest** misconceptions about personal branding. people think the goal is to get as many people as possible to see your content. it isn’t (!!) the goal is to get the right people to remember you.

**think about how hiring actually works**

imagine you’re a hiring manager. you have a role open, you post it, you get 400 applications. and then, while scrolling linkedin, you see someone whose name you’ve seen 15 times over the past 3 months. you recognise them, you know what they talk about, you’ve seen them share thoughtful opinions about your industry, maybe you’ve even interacted with them once or twice, and then you see their application. which person do you think feels more familiar: a) the person whose cv appeared in your inbox 5 minutes ago, or b) the person you’ve subconsciously been building a picture of for 3 months? this is the part of personal branding that doesn’t show up in analytics. familiarity. and familiarity is **ridiculously powerful.**

**the people who**_**“randomly”**_**get opportunities usually aren’t that random**

someone messages you about a job, asks you to speak at an event, wants to collaborate, or asks whether you’re available for freelance work. from the outside it looks like _“wow, they’re so lucky,”_ but often there’s been months of invisible work behind that moment. they’ve been posting, commenting, sharing ideas and showing up in the same conversations. the person who eventually sends the dm may have been watching for weeks, you just didn’t know it at the time.

that’s why i always say: **your audience is bigger than your follower count.** it’s everyone quietly watching. the recruiter who never likes your posts. the founder who reads every newsletter. the marketing director who keeps seeing your name. the person who hasn’t followed you but has clicked your profile 3 times. you don’t know they’re there, but they do.

**so what should you post?**

this is where i think people make personal branding far more complicated than it needs to be. you need to become associated with something, **not** everything (!!) if i see your name, what should i immediately think:_“she’s the person who talks about b2b content,” “he’s obsessed with creator marketing,” “they always have interesting takes on ai,” “she knows loads about paid social.”_ that’s positioning. and once you’ve decided what you want to be known for, your content should repeatedly reinforce it.

not every post needs to be groundbreaking. in fact it probably shouldn’t be. but what you do need is repetition, because the first time someone sees your opinion, they might scroll past. the fifth time, they start recognising it. the tenth time, they associate you with it. the twentieth time, you’re the person they think of when that topic comes up. that’s when your personal brand starts becoming an asset.

**you don’t need everyone (!!)**

this is something i wish more early-career marketers understood. you don’t need 100,000 followers. you don’t even necessarily need 10,000. if you’re trying to get a job in marketing, imagine having 300 people in the industry who know exactly who you are and what you’re good at. that’s powerful if 50 founders know you as “the person who understands social media,” that’s powerful, right?! if 20 hiring managers recognise your name, that’s powerful. if the right people know you exist, you’ve already won a **huge** part of the battle.

so yes, chase growth if you enjoy it, but don’t confuse reach with leverage. your goal isn’t to become famous, it’s to become known for something by the people who matter to you. and if you’re starting from zero right now, please don’t underestimate those first 100 people. they are not _“only 100,”_ they’re your first network, your first community, your first proof, your first opportunities, and potentially the people who change your career.

that’s exactly why i built The Marketing Lab around visibility rather than vanity metrics, because i don’t want marketers to become influencers, i want them to become known.
