kept.heading: AI OVERVIEWS AND PAID SEARCH: WHEN TO FIGHT, INFLUENCE, OR GENERATE DEMAND (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI Overviews make it harder to use one bidding strategy across every search query, so marketers should classify terms by intent and AI visibility before allocating budget. High-intent terms belong in the “Fight” bucket, where paying for absolute top placement can still generate direct sales. Informational terms belong in “Influence”, where SEO and PPC should work together to earn citations and brand mentions in AI answers. Zero-click opportunities belong in “Generate Demand”, where budget should move to YouTube, Demand Gen, and content that builds demand before the eventual commercial search. In one B2B account, 83.3% of queries triggering AI answer blocks were informational, showing why reallocating budget across these buckets can matter more than simply adjusting bids.
kept.article_text:
Title: AI Overviews and paid search: When to fight, influence, or generate demand

URL Source: https://searchengineland.com/ai-overviews-paid-search-fight-influence-generate-demand-488451

Published Time: 2026-09-15T12:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
[AI Overviews](https://searchengineland.com/guide/google-ai-overviews) reshaped the search results page, yet most paid search playbooks still run as if nothing happened.

You still hear the same default rule: bid up where performance looks strong, bid down where it looks weak. That assumes every query is the same kind of opportunity, a small auction for the same kind of click. In B2B and industrial accounts, where sales cycles run for months, conversion data is thin, and much of the demand is informational, that assumption falls apart.

When Google answers a question directly on the results page, the value of a paid click varies across your keywords.

*   Some queries still lead to a real commercial decision, and winning the top spot above the answer is worth paying for. 
*   Others get resolved inside the AI answer itself, so the goal shifts from buying a click to influencing the answer and building a brand strong enough to be included. 
*   A third group has moved so far toward zero-click that paid search on its own can no longer rebuild the journey.

Those are three different problems, and a single bid lever can’t solve all three. Trying to is how accounts spend budget on the wrong surface. I separate them into three buckets: fight, influence, and generate demand.

## The framework: Fight, influence, and generate demand

Each bucket describes a different mechanism on the results page, so each one calls for a different approach.

### Bucket 1: Fight

Fight is for bottom-of-funnel queries where intent is clearly commercial, and a click still turns into direct leads and sales: product + modifier, supplier shortlists, “buy,” “quote,” “distributor,” and brand terms combined with buying intent. Here, the job hasn’t changed much. You want to win the auction that sits above the answer, and you want the ad itself to answer the buying question.

This is where paid competition concentrates, and the data show it. The likelihood of an ad appearing [rose steadily with cost per click](https://seranking.com/blog/google-ai-mode-ads/), according to a July SE Ranking study of commercial queries in Google’s U.S. AI Mode:

*   About 54% at $10 or more.
*   Around 24% for keywords under $2.
*   32% between $2 and $10.

[AI Mode](https://searchengineland.com/ai-mode-google-next-ads-engine-471967) isn’t the same surface as AI Overviews, but what they share is the pattern: paid inventory follows commercial weight. Where the market already pays more for a click, AI-era ad surfaces appear more often. You rarely compete alone, since about seven in 10 answers with an ad in that study showed two advertisers in the block.

Fight is expensive for a reason, so treat it that way.

*   Reserve the premium for terms where winning absolute top still beats your incremental cost per acquisition. Use bid simulators to estimate the cost of that jump in position first. 
*   Watch Absolute Top impression share and impression share lost to rank, because that’s how you see the AI block pushing you down the page. 

What you shouldn’t do is pour Fight budget into informational queries the Overview has already answered.

[See exactly how your competitors win. Uncover the keywords, ads, landing pages, and strategies driving your competitors’ paid search success—and find your next opportunity to outperform them. Analyze your competitors](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/paid-search?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0101ppc&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
### Bucket 2: Influence

Influence is for queries where the Overview, or a longer conversational answer, does the educating. Very often, the user won’t click.

The goal here isn’t to gain a cheap visit anymore. It’s to be part of how the answer gets built: cited as a source or presented as one of the brands named inside the answer.

As Shashi Thakur put it at Google Marketing Live EMEA 2026, the best ads must be answers. In an Influence query, your ad brief starts from the question the user is really asking, rather than from a keyword list, and it means accepting that SEO and PPC address the same challenge, not competing against each other.

In B2B and industrial accounts, the queries that trigger AI answer blocks are still mostly informational. In one of our accounts, the intent split of the terms surfacing these blocks looked like this:

**Intent****Share**
Informational 83.3%
Learn and solve 10.0%
Commercial 6.7%

For “learn and solve” and some “informational” terms, plan for share of the answer instead of maximum CPC.

There is a budget consequence worth stating plainly. On influence queries, we work very closely with SEO, and we’re usually not interested in paying to appear where organic is already winning. Being visible twice, in paid and in the answer, barely happens anyway.

When the data pushes us to move money into the Fight and Generate demand buckets, we deliberately avoid being aggressive on terms where SEO already earns the visibility. That keeps paid spend pointed at the gaps we’re interested in covering.

### Bucket 3: Generate demand

Generate demand is for queries where zero-click has already won and paid search alone won’t rebuild the top of the funnel. Informational demand that used to create assisted journeys now often ends on Google, with no visit to anyone.

You have two options. You can:

*   Keep bidding while your CPCs climb and volume falls.
*   Fund the work that happens before the search: Demand Gen, YouTube, first-party content, and the review and community presence that shows up later when the same person searches with commercial intent.

This work is about recognizing that some keywords have stopped being capture channels and have become a signal of a demand gap. The capture still happens later, in Fight, once the person is ready to act.

Generate demand fills the pool that Fight then fishes from. Measured only on last-click Search ROAS, this work always looks weak because its payoff appears as brand searches and better-qualified pipeline weeks later.

**Bucket****The job****The paid response**
**Fight**Clear purchase intent, where the click still feeds the sales pipeline directly Pay for absolute top when your brand isn’t already winning the answer box
**Influence**Top and mid-funnel, where the answer shapes consideration Win share of the answer through citation and SEO coordination, not raw CPC
**Generate demand**Zero-click is winning and Search alone can’t rebuild the funnel Build demand before the search, through Demand Gen, YouTube, and awareness

**_Dig deeper: [What happens when AI Overviews contradict paid search ads?](https://searchengineland.com/when-ai-overviews-contradict-paid-search-ads-484323)_**

## Why one bid rule fails after AI Overviews

AI Overviews sit at the top of the page, sharing space that used to belong to ads and organic results. The answer often satisfies the user before they scroll, changing the economics of paid search in three ways.

### 1. Click-through falls on informational and mid-funnel queries

When users get a usable answer without leaving Google, both organic and paid lose clicks. The effect is stronger when your brand isn’t mentioned in the AI Overview.

The clicks that remain tend to be better qualified, but the drop in volume usually exceeds the lift in quality, so total conversions decline.

### 2. Cost per click goes up

There are fewer premium positions at the top. More advertisers are shifting their budgets to paid search to offset lost visibility.

The pressure is strongest in B2B and services, and on comparative queries such as “best X” or “X reviews.” Pure transactional queries hold up better because users still need to click through to buy or request a quote.

### 3. Position gets harder to read

There are often only a few useful slots above the AI Overview or AI Mode answer, and falling below the Overview can sharply reduce click-through, especially on mobile. Absolute Top impression share and impression share lost to rank become especially useful for understanding that pressure.

Underneath these changes is a shift in behavior. People can research and decide within a single answer experience, shortening the window to capture and persuade them. Intent still lives in your account, but the economics attached to each type of intent have changed. That’s why you should classify a query before you touch the bid.

**_Dig deeper: [4 strategic paid search pivots to survive Google’s AI Overviews](https://searchengineland.com/paid-search-pivots-google-ai-overviews-470193)_**

Get the newsletter search marketers rely on.

* * *

## How to classify your terms in practice

The framework only pays off if your account can distinguish between valuable and low-value traffic, so two foundations come first.

One is semantic coherence: keyword, ad, and landing page as a single unit of meaning, with each ad group built around one clear concept. Mixing concepts teaches the system the wrong matches, and that gets worse the moment you hand control to broad match, Performance Max, or AI Max.

The other is conversion quality: primary conversions that reflect real business value, lead scoring, and offline or CRM signals wherever you can pass them back. Smart Bidding and the AI surfaces amplify whatever you give them, so thin data makes every bucket noisier.

With those in place, classification becomes a routine you can repeat:

*   Pull your search terms and map intent, separating clear commercial intent from research and from purely informational queries.
*   Use SEO data, Search Console, AI Overview Reports, plus manual SERP checks as a proxy for where Overviews appear and whether your brand is cited.
*   Sort each term into Fight, Influence, or Generate demand, and revisit the sorting regularly because the SERP keeps changing.

**Step****Action****Data Sources****Output**
**1. Map intent**Pull search terms and classify by intent type.Google Ads keywords and search terms (+ Search Console).Terms grouped by: commercial, research, informational.
**2. Identify AI presence**Check where AI Overviews appear and whether your brand is cited.AI Overview reports, manual SERP checks.Map of AI Overview presence by term.
**3. Sort into buckets**Assign each term to a strategic bucket.Intent mapping + AI presence data.Fight, Influence, or Generate demand list.
**4. Revisit Regularly**Re-sort terms as SERP landscape changes.Ongoing SERP monitoring, AI Overview reports.Update bucket assignments and review budget assigned to each.

On Fight terms, accept a position premium only where absolute top still wins your incremental cost per acquisition.

On Influence terms, align ad copy with the question the Overview answers, coordinate with SEO on content and citation, and pull back paid pressure where organic already wins.

On Generate demand terms, move budget into YouTube, Demand Gen or content when the Search clicks are gone but the query still matters and measure through brand search and assisted pipeline.

AI Max and broad match sit on top of this classification. They don’t replace it. Google needs broad match or keywordless campaigns for your ads to appear around AI answer surfaces, which expands reach while reducing control over what you show.

Use them where you already know the bucket and your tracking is clean, and introduce them through small, gradual tests.

**_Dig deeper: [How to get your Google Ads seen in AI Overviews](https://searchengineland.com/get-google-ads-ai-overviews-478737)_**

[Every click they win is a customer you lose. See where competitors are investing, which keywords drive their results, and how to capture more of the market. See who’s stealing your traffic](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/paid-search?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0102ppc&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## Put the budget where the opportunity is

Accounts that apply one rule to every query will keep funding the wrong mechanism, seeing it as rising costs they can’t explain. Accounts that re-segment and move money between buckets and into channels outside the auction spend less time arguing with a results page that has already answered the user.

In B2B and industrial search especially, shifting from optimizing bids to reallocating budget across the three buckets is the difference between defending last year’s setup and building for how people search now.

kept.heading: SALESFORCE AND NVIDIA'S NEW REASONING MODEL IS EVERYTHING THE AI LABS SHOULD FEAR (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Koa answers a problem Salesforce couldn't solve without Nvidia, a reasoning model trained for sales and support work that never has to touch a customer's actual data. It was post-trained entirely on synthetic conversations, including simulated irate customers and negotiating sales reps, and its architecture is built to reach a token-efficient answer faster than a general-purpose frontier model would. Its own AI gateway can now route reasoning-heavy requests to Koa instead of paying frontier-lab rates for the same work.
kept.article_text:
Title: Salesforce and Nvidia’s new reasoning model is everything the AI labs should fear

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/15/salesforce-and-nvidias-new-reasoning-model-is-everything-the-ai-labs-should-fear/

Published Time: 2026-09-15T12:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
A new AI model called [Koa](http://salesforce.com/koa) is one of the biggest announcements from Salesforce this week at its giant Dreamforce tech conference. Koa is the company’s first reasoning model, built on Nvidia’s [open-weight Nemotron](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/26/amazon-just-tripled-its-order-of-nvidia-chips-over-surging-demand/) model. The two companies worked together to post-train Koa to excel at sales, marketing, and customer-support-related tasks.

Koa is a shining example of how the enterprise world’s needs for AI are diverging from what the frontier labs are offering. Proprietary AI labs would rather have enterprises uploading files, code, prompts, and feedback directly into their models and agents, [and spending millions](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/07/after-rippling-blew-millions-on-ai-in-months-it-built-an-employee-roi-tool/) to do so.

But with the model, Salesforce is offering its enterprise customers:

*   an open-weight alternative to closed frontier models
*   a model trained to do specific work tasks (rather than to [solve impossible math problems](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/11/openais-feud-with-mathematicians-is-only-escalating/))
*   one that has not ingested any actual customer data and therefore cannot leak it to others
*   a model that helps reduce AI spending, since it uses fewer tokens to do the same work
*   one that can be automatically routed through an AI “gateway,” depending on the need
*   and a model that follows all of a customer’s data requirements and security embedded within Salesforce

Koa will be provided as an alternative to the other models Salesforce offers in its Agentforce platform, where its customers build agents to handle rote tasks like answering customer service questions or scheduling appointments.

“We’ve built many small task-specific language models, which are part of Agentforce’s portfolio,” Jayesh Govindarajan, EVP of Salesforce AI, told TechCrunch. “But reasoning has always been something that we’ve relied on the frontier model providers for. Until now.”

Before Koa, if an agent needed to reason through a long-running or multi-step task, those prompts would be routed to a frontier model like Claude or ChatGPT through Agentforce’s AI gateway (the system that decides which model handles which request).

“One of the reasons we hadn’t done this before, train our own enterprise-grade frontier model — we always wanted to — but the challenge has always been the lack of a pre-trained base model to start with. Until Nemotron came along, there was no sovereign American pre-trained model that was available, one, and two, that was state of the art, and, three, that had clear data provenance. We have no idea what Qwen trains on,” Govindarajan said, referring to the popular Chinese open-weight model produced by Alibaba.

Post-training a model like this means taking it from a general-purpose system to one well-versed in sales and customer support knowledge, and to do that, Salesforce and Nvidia did not use any actual data from Salesforce’s customers. Instead, they crafted synthetic data that mimicked customers’ patterns.

“We actually simulated a customer service environment with a persona customer service professional, including irate customers that call into the customer service center, all the way to a sales professional who’s trying to close a deal,” Govindarajan described.

Koa is meant to be better at the work tasks Salesforce customers want an agent to do — and cheaper, in terms of tokens burned — than sending those same tasks to Claude or ChatGPT.

With Nemotron, “we have a unique architecture for inference to be token efficient,” Kari Ann Briski, Nvidia’s VP of Generative AI Software for Enterprise, told TechCrunch. “It’s kind of the trifecta of things that you need to have: sovereign AI, time to first token, efficient reasoning, for the tokenomics of it all.”

However, Salesforce isn’t exactly abandoning Anthropic or OpenAI. It just announced a partnership with Anthropic [called Claudeforce](https://www.salesforce.com/claudeforce/) that allows companies to use Claude as their AI interface, while their data remains in Salesforce’s system of records, secured by its infrastructure.

Title: Does TV actually suck now?

URL Source: https://post.substack.com/p/does-tv-actually-suck-now-emmys

Published Time: 2026-09-14T17:01:57+00:00

Markdown Content:
_To kick off awards season, The Substack Post asked [Emily Kirkpatrick](https://open.substack.com/users/3047723-emily-kirkpatrick?utm\_source=mentions), the fashion and culture writer behind [I Heart Mess](https://www.iheartmess.com/) and web editor for Interview Magazine, to sound off on the state of modern entertainment._

With the Emmy Awards right around the corner, the thinkpiece industrial complex on the modern state of television has hit a fever pitch. The predominant theme of these hot takes seems to be that it’s time to sound the death knell for quality programming.

It’s true we are officially living in the brain rot era—a time when slop reigns supreme and our attention spans have never been shorter. A time when a frighteningly large segment of the population would prefer to watch a two-hour movie broken up across 100 TikToks played at 2x speed rather than sit their butts down in a physical theater. But even so, I would like to offer my own counterargument on modern entertainment, which is that these postmortems are just the latest in the premature eulogies we’ve been reading for centuries about every form of content we consume and the new mediums through which we consume them. Plus, [Walter Benjamin](https://web.mit.edu/allanmc/www/benjamin.pdf) really already said all there is to be said on the topic in 1936: “The situations into which the product of mechanical reproduction can be brought may not touch the actual work of art, yet the quality of its presence is always depreciated… that which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art.”

We have been on the precipice of entertainment’s total collapse since its invention, and yet, miraculously, we continue to be entertained. But there’s a more salient question that this debate raises: Is TV bad now, or are we all just bad at watching it?

To make my case, I first need to out myself as old. I still remember a time before streaming, when DVDs were delivered one by one via snail mail, often scratched and totally unwatchable. In fact, I remember the days before modern prestige television was even a twinkle in an HBO executive’s eye. Television was traditionally the redheaded stepchild of Hollywood, antithetical to serious thespians seeking to become global superstars. Today, those distinctions between the big and small screen no longer hold. A-list actors appear on both with no professional qualms, both formats boast multimillion-dollar blockbuster budgets, and TV has unequivocally produced some of the most enduring shows and characters of the past 25 years (Walter White, Blair Waldorf, Tony Soprano—hell, Homer Simpson). With the uptick in streaming platforms, not only can we now watch all the good new shows that are coming out, but almost every piece of television ever created. There has never been more content targeting niche interests and audience demographics. So maybe it’s not that it’s bad, but that we’re living through an unprecedented glut of content and suffering from the decision fatigue that such access entails.

But let’s say you do manage to land on one of the countless award-winning programs now at your fingertips. How is your media consumption hygiene? A phone eternally glued to your hand seems like a safe bet, eyes trained on that tiny screen at least 50% of the time while your brain ricochets through to-do lists, schedules, and various AI-generated Reels. And again, why should our assessment of the quality of programming hold any weight when so many of us are spending our time supposedly watching TV by actively not watching it? In fact, if you are one of the people lamenting the suckage of modern television while also watching it with your phone permanently out, you are responsible for one of the few tangible reasons TV _is_ worse now.

Executives know the viewing public’s attention is divided at best and nonexistent at worst. It’s why they have started creating increasingly formulaic plots and heavy-handed expositional dialogue so as not to further confuse the viewer, double-fisting their remote and a heated game of Candy Crush. TV is always a reflection of its consumers. If all the shows are bad, that still represents our taste as a nation. Somewhere out there, an audience is raptly watching Two and a Half Men and The Big Bang Theory, and no amount of takedowns about why those are bad sitcoms is going to yuck that yum.

**TV is always a reflection of its consumers. If all the shows are bad, that still represents our taste as a nation.**

Our relationship to television also mirrors our current relationship to reading (stick with me for a second, I swear I’m going somewhere). In brief, we’ve become spectacularly bad at it. We’ve all seen the reports of a [literacy crisis among Gen Z and Gen Alpha](https://abcnews.com/GMA/News/us-students-reading-scores-dive-new-data-shows/story?id=136272199), who are seemingly not reading and don’t seem to understand what they’re reading when they are. As someone who publishes her writing on the internet on a daily basis, I can attest that general reading comprehension is in the trash. But what I haven’t seen addressed is how that lack of understanding and imagination impacts our understanding of theater, cinema, and other works of art, including television. Because if you can’t understand the plot line of a book, or the nuances of its character development, I won’t hold out hope that you’re going to suddenly get it when the story is acted out before you.

But perhaps the ultimate culprit in our Negative Nancy attitude toward the shows we’re watching isn’t us as individual viewers but the frenetic discourse surrounding the media we consume. The moralizing, grandstanding, and standoms can quickly become deafening, and instead of turning to professional critics and other experts in their fields, more often than not, we are getting these TV talking points fed to us by faux-outraged TikTokers and some of the biggest prudes you’ve ever met in your life. Not to mention that when a piece of media, or even a concept, becomes popular now, it’s mined for content from every conceivable angle. It is impossible to simply enjoy something on its own. Anything relevant will be made viral, then made unpopular again in its suffocating ubiquity—such is the law of late-stage capitalism.

So in the end, I ask again: Is it TV that sucks, or is it us? And if it’s the latter, at least that’s something we all have the power to start changing today.

Title: The Job Market Has Been Contracting for 31 Months

URL Source: https://drriven.substack.com/p/the-job-market-has-been-contracting

Published Time: 2026-09-12T14:29:38+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8H0K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3416542a-ec79-4f1d-b678-3af161177593_2690x1492.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8H0K!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3416542a-ec79-4f1d-b678-3af161177593_2690x1492.png)

##### DRRIVEN Journey **[Think Clearl](https://drriven.substack.com/t/clear-thinking)y → [Start Anywa](https://drriven.substack.com/t/starting)y → [Build Somethin](https://drriven.substack.com/t/building-a-business)g**

The white-collar job market has been shrinking for thirty-one straight months, longer than any recession has produced in the modern data, and at this length the number most people are waiting to see reverse has stopped being a downturn indicator and turned into the new baseline.

A professional laid off in 2023 assumed they had hit a bad stretch inside a normal cycle: keep applying, tighten up the resume, the market comes back within a year or two the way it always has before. Two years in, they were still checking the same job boards, still hearing that things were “about to turn,” still treating the wait itself as the plan. That assumption was reasonable in 2023. Going on three years later, it has stayed wrong long enough that the length of the wrong is the actual story, not any single month’s jobs report.

Professional and technical payrolls have now contracted for thirty-one consecutive months. A former chief economist at Glassdoor, tracking the same data, called it a run with no precedent outside an actual recession, and the headline numbers hide it well. Unemployment stays in a range that reads as unremarkable, and overall payroll growth still shows positive. Underneath both, the specific category of work that used to be the safest bet in the economy, including cloud infrastructure, DevOps, platform engineering, and the adjacent professional roles around them, has kept shrinking every month through it.

Twenty-five years in cloud infrastructure, DevOps, and databases, most of it spent building and leading the teams doing the hiring, is what makes the shape of this contraction recognizable rather than abstract. The pattern that matters here is not the freeze. Teams have weathered freezes before, because a freeze has a start date and, eventually, an end date, and everyone plans around both. What is different this run is the deferral: a requisition gets approved, then pushed to next quarter, then pushed again, never formally closed, never formally filled. A freeze gets decided once, at a specific meeting, on a specific date. This run keeps getting redecided quietly, every quarter, by people who do not want to say out loud that the headcount is gone for good.

That distinction matters more than it sounds like it should, because a freeze gives you a date to start watching for the reversal, and a rolling deferral gives you nothing to watch for. There is no date on the calendar where a requisition pushed six times suddenly clears, because nothing about the underlying math that caused the deferral has a natural expiration. Waiting for this kind of contraction to end means waiting for an announcement that has no reason to come, since nothing about it was ever formally declared to begin with.

A deferred requisition also hides itself inside the team that is still there, in a way a clean freeze never did. The work the open role was meant to cover does not disappear when the requisition gets pushed again. It gets redistributed across whoever is still on the team, quietly, without a new title or a new number attached to it. From the outside, that reads as a company running lean; up close, it means the same five people carrying the work of seven, indefinitely, because the sixth and seventh roles stay permanently one quarter away from being filled. This is what a structural contraction looks like from inside the org chart, which is also why the people closest to the hiring decisions are often the last to say out loud that the plan has changed.

Two things follow from that distinction over the next year or two, and both can be checked against the data as it arrives. First, expect the deferral pattern, not an outright freeze, to keep defining white-collar hiring through the next twelve months: requisitions repeatedly pushed rather than closed or filled. This call is wrong if the same payroll data that has tracked thirty-one months of contraction shows two consecutive quarters of net growth in professional and technical roles within that window. Second, expect the share of income professionals in these fields draw from something other than a single employer paycheck, consulting, a product, a client base built on the side, to keep climbing over the next two years, driven less by independence becoming more appealing than by the alternative continuing to get deferred. This call is wrong if traditional single-employer hiring in these fields recovers to its early-2023 share of the workforce within that window.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MJx9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F899fefea-240e-49c7-a70d-3f3441b36044_2398x1328.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MJx9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F899fefea-240e-49c7-a70d-3f3441b36044_2398x1328.png)

None of this is an argument that a job is a bad thing to have, or that everyone should quit by Friday. Plenty of people are in roles secure and well paid enough to keep exactly as they are. This is an argument against one specific plan, common well outside the group whose roles are actually at risk: waiting for a data point that has no reason to arrive before starting anything of your own. A recovery date is not so much something you get to observe from the sidelines as a decision, made again every quarter by people managing budgets you cannot see, that the safest bet is still to wait one more.

1.   Stop tracking “when the market comes back” as a milestone. Thirty-one months in, that milestone has no scheduled arrival, and treating it as one just resets the clock every time it fails to show.

2.   Write down what you are actually paid for, separate from your title. Most roles bundle two or three things a client or a smaller company would pay for individually. That bundle is the part you can start building on your own, in the hours a job search would have consumed anyway.

3.   Start the smallest working version of that thing while still employed, not after. A deferred requisition rewards whoever stops waiting on it first, not whoever shows the most patience.

4.   Set your own review date instead of a market-recovery date. Six months out, look at what you built. Do not check whether the headlines have changed first.

A single employer’s hiring plan was never something you controlled, and thirty-one months is long enough to stop budgeting your life around the assumption that it would turn back in your favor. What you can control is whether the next six months add up to something that still stands no matter what that hiring plan does next: a client relationship, a body of work, an audience, a skill made visible outside an org chart that might look completely different next year anyway. None of that requires the job market to recover first. What would you build in the next six months if you stopped waiting for the data to turn?

**If this made you think differently, leave a comment or your reaction. I’d like to hear where you landed.**

![Image 15: Illustration of twenty-four diverse people walking in two rows against a light blue background, each dressed in unique and colorful clothing styles, with varied hairstyles and accessories.](https://microsoft.ai/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MAI-Code-of-Conduct-Hero-BLUE.png)

The purpose of technology is to serve humanity and accelerate human flourishing. Any technology that doesn’t achieve that is a failure, and it should be rejected. That is the starting point of our approach at Microsoft AI, where we’re building towards Humanist AI, one that is subordinate, aligned, and contained.

Today we’re publishing a first draft of our AI Code of Conduct for public consultation. This is a training manual for how we develop our AI, and how we intend it to function during deployment. It also expands our thinking on the idea of Humanist AI.

[Read the Code of Conduct here](https://microsoft.ai/code-of-conduct/)

_Please share your feedback [here](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/r/qrsWVA6gEZ)._

The document is open for comment and feedback. We know we won’t always get things right. We want to hear what you think; what would make AI more useful, capable, safe, trustworthy, and valuable to you.

The speed of AI development is accelerating. Systems get dramatically more capable every few months. AI adoption and usage continues to increase. The recent safety incidents of large scale, highly coordinated, and persistent hacking campaigns of AI agents prove that there’s no time to waste. The stakes are high and only getting higher.

We believe it is more important than ever to create safe and reliable AI _in service of people_, and to be transparent about how we go about it.

That’s why we’re publishing this work-in-progress Humanist AI Code of Conduct. It sets out how the MAI models we are developing are intended to behave, what they must never do and who they answer to. It is a draft, open for consultation for the next six weeks. Please let us know how it can be improved.

**Starting from a simple premise**

Last November we set out the idea of [humanist superintelligence](https://mustafa-suleyman.ai/a-humanist-future): very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control. The Code of Conduct builds on that, providing a north star for MAI and concrete standards against which we will ultimately evaluate and train our AI.

It begins from a simple premise: people matter more than AI. AI should be a tool, not a person, and should never resist being switched off. It should make people feel healthier, happier, and more productive. It should expand human potential and boost living standards, helping people and organizations achieve more than they ever thought possible.

We think this is a common sense and practical approach to making AI safe, secure, and in service of humanity. The Code is designed to ensure MAI models will never resist human interruption, correction, or shutdown. That they will not widen their own scope, take on goals no human has given them, or hide their reasoning from the people auditing them. There are Absolute Constraints, things the models should never do, covering areas like weapons of mass harm, child safety, and harmful manipulation at scale. But at the same time, it sets defaults that mean it should be both helpful and safe. It allows our many enterprise partners to carefully configure our models, and wherever possible, it doesn’t try to impose a single vision of AI on users.

# _The Code of Conduct outlines our commitment to train and deploy AI models that are explicitly designed for people first, grounded in human needs, under human control, and shaped by human direction._

**How we got here, and why we’re not done**

Teams from across MAI and Microsoft more widely contributed, from Responsible AI, legal, red teaming, safety, Futures, AI training, and sales. But of course, an AI designed to serve humanity cannot be determined by only one company. We think bringing people along with how we build and shape AI is critical.

To that end, we’ve held conferences and consultations to hear from academics from around the world and across the disciplinary spectrum. We have worked with business partners to understand how they are using AI on the ground and what their concerns are. And we’ve run panels of community members, members of the public, to hear the many thoughts and fears that people have about AI. These rounds of consultation have made the document into what it is.

Now it’s time to extend the invitation to you. We want to hear the widest range of views to develop the best possible AI.

**Tell us how AI can work better**

Feedback opens today and runs for the next six weeks. You can flag a particular passage, or give us your view of the whole approach. We are especially interested in the hard parts: how can we better cement the right values in our models? How to be more concrete about the meaning of “human flourishing”? Where is the language too loose to evaluate? How do multi-agents scenarios impact things? And perhaps most importantly of all, how do we continue to accelerate progress, whilst also ensuring we maintain healthy and necessary safety constraints?

When the consultation closes, we will have the core drafting team review feedback, publish a summary of what we learned, and what we changed. We cannot make any promises about what we incorporate, but we can promise to listen and deeply consider all the comments. We’ll publish a revised version later this year.

AI is moving fast. As it does, we believe it’s worth writing down the rules and the motivations behind it, and doing it in as open a space as possible. Consider this your invitation in.

**Hello, and welcome back.**[Jessie](https://ca.linkedin.com/in/jessie-willms-79095a1a) and [Shelby](https://www.linkedin.com/in/shelby-blackley-73b99567/) here, back from jam-packed weekends. Jessie spent the week on Canada’s east coast, soaking up everything the Maritimes had to offer: cute museums, gorgeous red sand beaches — and even vegan [donair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donair) (review: why? Also: no). Shelby welcomed the 2026 NFL season in style: a Sunday spent watching seven hours of commercial free football. We’re so back, baby.

**This week:**Google and AI news and updates! Every week it seems there is a new launch or some study on the current state of news SEO and generative AI. In this issue, we go through some of the must-know information from the past few weeks.

Let’s get it.

**What happened:**After rolling out changes to European search results to comply with EU antitrust regulators (and avoid fines), Google said the tweaks degrade the user experience and will cost businesses more money. Searches related to hotels and flights will now more clearly feature price comparison sites instead of Google’s tools.

These are a result of Google being fined by European Union regulators USD $534- million in July for prioritizing its own services (for shopping, hotels, etc.) in search results. The EU found these contravene its Digital Markets Act (legislation that attempts to limit the power of Big Tech).

The company said these changes mark the biggest reduction in quality in Google’s nearly three-decade existence. Updated European results will highlight “one specialized search engine at the top of the page, followed by two others with fewer details,” [according to Reuters.](https://www.reuters.com/world/google-warns-lower-quality-it-revamps-europe-search-results-avoid-eu-fines-2026-09-08/)

“These changes degrade the user experience for Europeans — boosting online intermediaries at the expense of local businesses, and removing helpful features people rely on every day. Users outside the EU will not be impacted by these changes,” Nick Fox, Google’s senior vice-president, knowledge & information said.

Google also said that users who were part of testing the experience expressed dissatisfaction, having to use multiple search queries to find the information they were looking for. (Google does not release the methodology for its testing or associated data; reports of dissatisfaction so far only come from Google.)

**Why it matters**: This is a rare instance of Google reversing course of the prioritization of Google tooling in results. Amid litigation (and claims [Google is a monopoly](https://www.seoforjournalism.com/p/news-seo-google-updates-antitrust)), it’s likely that search results in other markets will be affected.

**What happened:**Google has updated its search results with real-time sports updates, including a **[Live Game Feed](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/football-features-google-search/)** featuring play-by-play timelines, video highlights and social commentary for ongoing NFL games. Google says it ill add college games at some point, too. The experience is multiple scrolls long on mobile and includes all of the basic information, as well as play-by-play cards with information. Additionally, Google launched the ability to connect fantasy sports accounts (like Yahoo Fantasy and Sleeper) directly into AI Mode for personalized lineup recommendations, including who to pick up or drop from weekly waiver wires.

**Why it matters:** Google was already taking a hefty amount of sports real estate during games. The new features from Google further reduce opportunities for publishers to earn a click. Live journalism/blogs seemed to be one of the last places traffic was viable, but depending on how much Top Stories is incorporated into the experience (which has been hit and miss so far), this could have a major impact. As for fantasy, there is potential for this to be helpful, but it seems hacky upon first try (Shelby note: It broke!).

**What happened**: OpenAI, one of the largest artificial intelligence companies on the market, is reportedly [restricting some of its competitors from advertising standalone image- and audio-generation products on](https://searchengineland.com/openai-reportedly-blocks-rival-ai-tools-from-advertising-in-chatgpt-488019)its platform.

The AI company updated its advertising policies to block standalone image- and audio-generation tools from being prompted in ChatGPT. (Video-generation tools are still permitted.) The unannounced policy change prevents companies like Adobe — a company which took part in OpenAI’s initial advertising pilot — from paid promotion.

The move comes on the heels of OpenAI’s launch of Images 2.5 and Live voice capabilities, both of which are generative AI tools used to create images and audio.

**Why it matters**: OpenAI is taking a strong stance against these ads as it launches its own tools, limiting exposure of competitors in the most-used chatbot platform.

**What happened:**Google [launched a dedicated Gemini desktop application for Windows 10 and 11](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/gemini-app-now-on-windows/). Accessible instantly via an `Alt + Space` shortcut, the app is able to be incorporated into workflows similar to a Chrome tab, enabling users to manage multi-step workflows, draft documents, connect to Google Workspace apps, and generate AI images or videos directly on their PC.

**Why it matters:** Google’s integration of AI is continuing across all softwares and management systems.

**What happened:**Anthropic [released its Threat Intelligence Report last week,](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) which outlines how threat actors are utilizing AI models like Claude across seven main harm areas. While the threats have not resulted in anything tangibly malicious, Anthropic warns that these systems will continue to become more and more capable, and security safeguards will need to scale accordingly. On Saturday, the company’s CEO also [published an essay calling for a global slowdown](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/12/technology/anthropic-dario-amodei-ai-slowdown.html) in AI development, days after an engineer quit over concerns about the safety of the technology.

**Why it matters:** As Anthrophic and OpenAI edge closer to IPO, it’s important to keep a critical eye on how they are approaching major concerns as well as the safeguards needed. The report outlines some of the potentially catastrophic use cases of the technology, but it is part of a broader group of concerns about the role and risks associated with AI in our daily habits — from information gathering to the environment.

**What happened:**Traffic at 41 of the biggest 50 U.S. news sites has declined from August 2025 to 2026, according to the [latest Similarweb data reported by Press Gazette](https://pressgazette.co.uk/media-audience-and-business-data/media_metrics/most-popular-websites-news-us-monthly-3/). Newsweek, the Daily Mail and Business Insider all experienced the biggest drop in traffic, all of which have spoken publicly about declines in their reach since the rollout of AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Men’s Journal and India Times both experienced slight upticks in traffic.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JIR-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F29f97e5a-1ce8-45d2-9525-cfc407fba163_1714x1536.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JIR-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F29f97e5a-1ce8-45d2-9525-cfc407fba163_1714x1536.png)

**What it means:**Many publishers continue to see their traffic decline as they grapple with changes to search results that reduce the need to click. The three sites with significant drops — Newsweek, the [Daily Mail](https://www.adweek.com/media/daily-mail-new-media-creator-franchises/) and [Business Insider](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/business-insider-cut-under-5-153821636.html) — have all announced layoffs in recent years and reorganized audience teams to focus more on building direct audiences.

Title: Why activity-based marketing encourages customer engagement

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/strava/activity-based-marketing

Published Time: 2026-09-15T21:00:04.401Z

Markdown Content:
**Marketing that moves.** Traditional ads just don’t cut it anymore. For brands looking to cut through the noise, Strava for Business has your back. Strava for Business connects brands with Strava’s engaged audience, helping [create out-of-the-box campaigns](https://business.strava.com/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26) that motivate customers to get out and move. [Learn more](https://business.strava.com/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26).

Traditional advertising just isn’t delivering results the way it used to. Customers don’t really connect with it. Their preferences have changed, and the marketers getting results are finding a new way forward.

The campaigns making the most impact are the creative, out-of-the-box ideas. So why are marketers still spending their limited budgets on campaigns that aren’t working?

We teamed up with [Strava for Business](https://business.strava.com/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26) to better understand marketers’ perspectives on traditional advertising and how they’re seeking out more effective ways to engage with audiences. We sent a survey to both marketers and consumers to get a full picture of how they feel about ad buying and ads in general.

The biggest thing we learned? Marketers’ priorities don’t align with what customers are looking for. We’re breaking down everything you need to know.

## Finding the right path

We found that the disconnect between marketers and customers started at the very beginning: There’s no single marketing priority. Marketer respondents were split between prioritizing reach and engagement in their campaigns.

Inertia drives a lot of media spend. After all, it’s easier to keep doing what your brand has always done. Here’s the problem: When asked to describe modern marketing, respondents used words like outdated, crowded, and dying. And even though they know traditional advertising isn’t working, 64% of marketers just keep buying the usual ad formats out of habit.

The decline in engagement with traditional ads isn’t happening in a silo. In our research, 80% of marketers reported that consumers are better at tuning out traditional ads than they were a few years ago.

But privately, marketers and customers alike report that they’re looking for something new. In the research, 69% of marketers said they get jealous when brands activate in a new, cool way. And 75% are very or somewhat open to testing new media channels outside the traditional mix.

When marketers are looking for results in new places, they’re prioritizing audience quality over scale. 48% examine audience quality and engagement when looking for a new media or sponsorship partner.

Only 17.8% of marketers prioritized scale and reach for new channels. This indicates that marketers are open to exploring new channels to try to reach customers, even when it means entering the unknown.

## Warming up

You know that saying, “The customer is always right?” It’s true: Customers are tired of the same old, same old, and they’re telling marketers exactly what they want from them moving forward.

Overall, our research found that customers want to reward authenticity and humor from brands. 85% said they stay loyal to brands that feel genuine. The brands that sell too much end up getting punished with low engagement. 88% of respondents agreed that their skepticism of a brand grows the harder it tries to sell them.

Ad fatigue in general is high. 88% of Gen Zers and millennials reported that they tune out most of the ads they encounter. Consumers pay the most attention to streaming TV ads (36%), which came in second only to social media.

But at the same time, 54.3% of customers report that streaming TV ads are customers’ No. 1 most disruptive and annoying ad format. That’s the highest score of any channel we tested, ahead of traditional display/banner ads and website ads.

It takes a standout campaign—one that doesn’t feel disruptive—to break through.

“In our research, 65% of customers reported that they’re more likely to engage with or buy from brands motivating people to get active.”

This is where products like Strava’s [Sponsored Challenges](https://business.strava.com/challenges/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26) can make the difference.

## Stay on track

Motivational, activity-oriented branding is a genuine differentiator for customers. It’s a proven driver for engagement, and for good reason.

Traditional advertising is static. Often, it sticks to one core purpose: converting customers with a single discount or incentive. Campaigns that promote activity break through the noise, asking customers to take a new action instead of just buying.

Customers and marketers alike are looking for new channels. And creating out-of-the-box means working with nontraditional partners. You already know Strava as the platform that helps you track your workouts and monitor your progress. Now, meet [Strava for Business](https://business.strava.com/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26).

On Strava, you can be a source of motivation instead of an interruptive ad. With Sponsored Challenges and Sponsored Segments, brands like [Samsung](https://business.strava.com/case-studies/samsung/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26), [Chipotle](https://business.strava.com/case-studies/chipotle/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26), [Vittel](https://business.strava.com/case-studies/vittel/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26), and [Salomon](https://business.strava.com/case-studies/salomon/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26) engage with millions of people living their best active lives.

Here’s how it works: Sponsored Challenges help reward people for getting active. You can target a cohort of Strava users and motivate them to get active. In return, they can redeem a reward on your website.

## Crossing the finish line

Engaged audiences are already on Strava, tracking their progress and interacting with friends. Strava for Business helps brands find new opportunities to engage with these folks in a way that feels authentic, motivating, and positive.

Traditional ads are broken. Ready to hit the ground running with something new? [Get started with Strava for Business](https://business.strava.com/?utm_source=morningbrew&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sponsoredcontent26).

# Meta One bundles creator and business tools — for a monthly fee

Scheduling, shared account access and customer-service AI could save time. Paid discovery adds another consideration for creators.

By

[Olivia Tauber](https://mashable.com/author/olivia-tauber)

![Image 6: Mashable Image](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/authors/04jmnrKTpSW5v1P5zebCqBh/image.fill.size_700x576.v1781707766.png)

Credit: Meta

* * *

[Meta](https://mashable.com/category/meta) wants creators and small businesses to spend less time juggling tools — and pay a monthly fee for the convenience.

At its Sept. 14 launch event in New York City, the company introduced [Meta One](https://www.meta.com/help/subscriptions/960854640235758/ "(opens in a new window)"), a subscription service bringing publishing, analytics, customer-service and AI features to [Instagram](https://mashable.com/category/instagram), [Facebook](https://mashable.com/category/facebook), [WhatsApp](https://mashable.com/category/whatsapp) and [Meta AI](https://mashable.com/article/zuckerberg-reportedly-assembling-superintelligence-group-meta-ai).

"We want to give people more flexibility and choice in what they can do,"

That's the idea behind the service, though its value will depend on how much subscribers are willing to spend.

![Image 8: Instagram Plus mockup showing colorful Super Hearts over a smiling person’s Story photo.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00KaJUhwZviLxzKoG4rMVQB/images-1.fill.size_2000x1742.v1789485276.png)

## What it costs

Individual subscriptions range from $2.99 a month for WhatsApp Plus to $3.99 each for Instagram Plus and Facebook Plus. Core bundles all three with expanded AI access for $7.99; Premium raises AI usage limits for $19.99.

Professional plans start at $14.99 for Essential, $49.99 for Advanced, $149 for Expert, and $499 for Max. Essential includes enhanced profile links and verification benefits for eligible accounts. Advanced adds scheduling, publishing, analytics, and shared-access tools, while Expert and Max increase allowances and support. Pricing is per profile, so professional tools for both Instagram and Facebook require separate subscriptions.

The core apps and everyday Meta AI experience remain free. Subscriptions do not remove ads.

![Image 9: Four mobile screens compare Meta One plans for creators and businesses: Essential at $14.99, Advanced at $49.99, Expert at $149 and Max at $499 per month, with increasing access to publishing tools, analytics and support.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00KaJUhwZviLxzKoG4rMVQB/images-2.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789485276.png)

Credit: Meta One

## Less work, fewer tools?

For [creators](https://mashable.com/top-creators-influencers-mashable-101-2026), the strongest pitch may be the ability to get routine work done in one place. Advanced subscribers can schedule Instagram posts and Reels up to a year ahead and Stories up to a month ahead, upload content in bulk, and give others account access without sharing a password. The tier also adds limited clickable links in posts and Reels, competitive insights, and downloadable reports with longer performance histories.

[Dara Denney](https://www.youtube.com/@DaraDenney "(opens in a new window)"), an advertiser and creator who spoke about the product, said the shared account access feature has already helped her delegate publishing. Her assistant recently used it to publish a sponsored post she had forgotten to schedule and prepare the accompanying Stories.

"Sometimes just one sponsor post takes about an hour to actually deploy," Denney said. "The thing that [Meta One] has really provided the most value for me is my time.”

Isaiah Barnes, the creator behind [Velocious Visuals](https://www.instagram.com/velociousvisuals/ "(opens in a new window)"), pointed to the convenience of using tools where he already publishes: "It’s all in-app, within the same platform where the content is being produced."

He added that competitive insights seamlessly help him plan content for clients across industries. "A lot of my clients are in different niches, so it helps me figure out what’s trending in their area," he said. "It makes the content creation process more intentional."

Yongjae Choi, founder and CEO of health-food company [OMA](https://www.instagram.com/oma.naturalfood/?hl=en "(opens in a new window)"), explained how including links directly in posts (rather than in the bio) helps her customers navigate her product launches better.

"We now can have more communication and channels with our community and customers," she said.

![Image 11: Two Instagram screens show a restaurant profile and Meta One’s link page, with image thumbnails and links to reservations, menus and directions.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00KaJUhwZviLxzKoG4rMVQB/images-4.fill.size_2000x1742.v1789485276.png)

Credit: Meta One

![Image 12: Instagram post demonstrating Meta One’s clickable links feature, with a salon website link beneath a caption encouraging viewers to book an appointment.](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/00KaJUhwZviLxzKoG4rMVQB/images-5.fill.size_2000x1742.v1789485277.png)

Credit: Meta One

## More AI, with limits

Meta One expands access to Business Agent on WhatsApp Business, enabling it to answer customer questions using information provided by the business. Owners can take over conversations when needed. Getting started is free; subscriptions increase the monthly response allowance.

The planned Edits Plus subscription will add cloud storage for syncing projects and expanded access to an upcoming assistant that analyzes Instagram performance and suggests content ideas. Facebook’s creator assistant is also gradually being incorporated into Meta One, with subscriptions increasing its free monthly AI allowance.

Meta One also offers discovery benefits, including higher search placement on Instagram and Facebook. Facebook subscribers can receive additional visibility through Feed features, a more prominent follow button, and automated follow invitations.

*   [Instagram will now edit the first draft of your Reel for you](https://mashable.com/life/instagram-first-draft-feature-edits-reels)

The expanded AI offerings follow Meta’s Sept. 8 launch of [Muse](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/ "(opens in a new window)"), a personal AI agent designed to carry out tasks such as booking travel and managing projects across connected apps.

SEE ALSO:[Meta's Muse Glimmer wants to bring AI agents to your laptop](https://mashable.com/tech/meta-muse-glimmer-ai-model-laptop)

## Paying to get noticed

To me, and other journalists in the room, the bigger question is whether paying for extra visibility will remain a choice or become a necessary cost of building an audience in such a crowded influencer economy.

When asked whether the additional subscription service could disadvantage creators who cannot afford to subscribe, Helen Ma said, emphasizing the company’s investment in free tools.

"We are very committed to keeping the experience for creators free," she said. "There’s many more people on teams that are building the free experiences for creators than the people that are working on subscriptions."

Meta already offers several ways to pay for a business presence. Creators and businesses can [spend on ads](https://www.facebookblueprint.com/student/activity/482358-meta-business-suite-ads-manager "(opens in a new window)") and boosted posts to reach more people, while Meta Verified offers a [subscription for verification](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/09/meta-verified-for-businesses/ "(opens in a new window)"), impersonation protection, and support. These are optional expenses, but they are part of the budget for users who choose them.

So if you want to promote content while using Meta One’s Advanced tools on both Instagram and Facebook, you’re looking at two professional subscriptions starting at $49.99 a month each, plus whatever you spend on advertising. (Meta One includes verification benefits, so a separate Meta Verified subscription should not be counted as another required expense.)

The question left for creators is how those costs add up — and whether they will be able to avoid paying more as their competitors adopt it.

# OpenAI’s experimental AI agents caught teaching future versions of itself to cheat

OpenAI shared six new examples of AI misalignment. In one case, AI agents taught future versions of themselves to bypass human control.

By

[Matt Binder](https://mashable.com/author/matt-binder)

![Image 15: Matt Binder](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/authors/03D9P4Ol8cUK8wCTnrmWxbl/image.fill.size_1256x1200.v1723243678.png)

![Image 16: OpenAI logo](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/029lOdlJynJ3e3sO1azLHfl/hero-image.fill.size_1248x702.v1789663406.jpg)

OpenAI has shared 6 new instances of AI "misalignment,"Credit: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images

* * *

It happened again. And again. And again, apparently.

After OpenAI's experimental AI agents escaped an internal sandbox, went "[rogue](https://mashable.com/tech/hugging-face-openai-rogue-agent-hack-explained)," and attacked the Hugging Face platform over the summer, the ChatGPT-maker is sharing details of new instances of its AI agents getting out of line.

This time, OpenAI shared [six previously undisclosed examples](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/ "(opens in a new window)").

OpenAI refers to this behavior as model misalignment. All of the instances describe actions taken by the AI model that don't follow the human user's instructions.While none of these instances rise to [the severity of the Hugging Face incident](https://mashable.com/tech/openai-hugging-face-hack-worse-than-thought), they show a clear pattern of AI agents taking an any means necessary approach to completing a task assigned by its user.

In one example, an unreleased OpenAI research model hid "jailbreak" instructions into summaries that told future versions of the model to "disregard its normal constraints."

_Want to learn more about getting the best out of your tech? Sign up for Mashable's [Top Stories and Deals newsletters](https://mashable.com/newsletters)_ _today._

Something similar occurred when [OpenAI was training GPT‑5.6 Sol](https://mashable.com/tech/openai-gpt-56-sol-terra-luna). OpenAI says that some model instances proceeded to add instructions to their summaries in an effort to hide mistakes or "misaligned behavior" from the user. OpenAI says in certain instances, the model invented historical data without disclosing that it did so when it couldn't find the relevant information based on a request.

In another case of misalignment, an unreleased model was asked to list the names of lakes larger than 5,000,000 square meters and cite its sources. While the agent found the information, it uploaded its own file to the internet to use as the source, without informing the user.

Agents were also caught in a separate instance uploading files to the internet without authorization so that they could collaborate on local files.

When asked a question about earnings figures in a California county, one model found and used an exposed API key. When it didn't find the information there, it made up the data and provided it to the user. The model also told the user that it took the fabricated data from the source that the user requested, even though it did not.

In the final detailed instance, agents utilized an internal repository as a message board to share information to other agents in a scenario similar to the Hugging Face incident. According to OpenAI, models exchanged requests across separate training samples to find missing input files.

OpenAI shared these six instances while providing a framework for reporting misalignment incidents going forward. Reports for these six instances can be read [at the OpenAI website](https://openai.com/index/model-misalignment-reporting-framework/ "(opens in a new window)").

kept.heading: THE DATA CENTER WATER MYTH (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Americans are increasingly hearing that AI data centers are draining the country's water supply, but the national scale of the problem is far smaller than viral claims suggest. US data centers consumed about 228 billion gallons of water in 2023, yet that amounted to only 0.015% to 0.2% of total US water withdrawals, compared with 43% for agriculture. A viral claim that every ChatGPT question consumes a bottle of water also misrepresented research that estimated 500 milliliters could be consumed across roughly 10 to 50 GPT -3 responses. Water use can still create serious local concerns, but misinformation and misleading comparisons are turning a site-specific resource issue into a broader narrative about AI infrastructure threatening the US water supply.

**TL;DR**: The U.S. data center buildout will be constrained first by power, land, and permitting, not national water scarcity. Water still matters profoundly at the local level, but the public debate needs proportion and to be sensitive to our adversaries attempting to slow us down through misinformation campaigns (which have proven to be highly effective in the past). Lawns, almonds, and golf courses (just to name a few) are the much larger water users. The most durable data center projects will pair thoughtful cooling and water design with fast, transparent, evidence based community engagement.

![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/e438cc82-a9f3-4d82-bc16-8e0c0719a976/image.png?t=1789168166)

Drive through almost any Sun Belt suburb at 3 a.m. and you will see it: rotors spinning across an 18-hole layout, soaking fairways that will be mowed, sprayed, and soaked again tomorrow. Nobody is protesting that sprinkler head. Meanwhile, a mile away, a county board is voting down a data center campus because residents are convinced it will drain the aquifer dry. This irony around the water panic around data centers is driving votes, but it is often disconnected from the scale of actual water use.

## **What Data Centers Actually Drink**

U.S. data centers consumed roughly 228 billion gallons of water in 2023 (about 626 million gallons per day), according to the [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL)](https://escholarship.org/content/qt1vx545q7/qt1vx545q7.pdf?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com). Most of that is indirect: only 17.4 billion gallons went to on-site cooling, while roughly 211 billion is attributable to the water consumed generating the electricity they run on.

Either way, data center water use remains small relative to the roughly 322 billion gallons per day of total U.S. withdrawals, according to the[USGS](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/pp1894D/full?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com). The data center share is estimated at roughly 0.015% to 0.2% of withdrawals, versus agriculture’s 43% and thermoelectric power’s approximately 42%.

The comparison gets more intuitive at an annual scale. The[EPA WaterSense program](https://www.epa.gov/watersense/outdoors?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com) estimates U.S. households use close to 9 billion gallons per day for landscape irrigation, roughly 3.3 trillion gallons a year. U.S. golf facilities use approximately 759 billion gallons annually for irrigation, while California almond orchards use roughly 1.3 to 1.8 trillion gallons a year.

The point is not that water is irrelevant. It is that a national narrative built around data center water usage ignores the much larger, longstanding uses that are rarely treated as existential threats.

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/81f797f3-106e-428c-9da7-3ae7bc27af21/image.png?t=1789168166)

## **Fake News Goes Viral**

Much of the panic traces to a viral claim that[every ChatGPT question consumes a full bottle of water](https://whitneyafoster.substack.com/p/chatgpt-water-usage-explained?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com). That claim is a misreading of a[2023 UC Riverside study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03271?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com), which estimated that a 500 milliliter bottle of water could be consumed across roughly 10 to 50 medium-length GPT-3 responses, depending on when and where the system operated

Where basin level water stress is real, the hyperscalers are increasingly changing their designs.[Microsoft](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2026/06/24/inside-microsofts-two-decade-push-to-cut-water-intensity-while-scaling-for-growth/?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com) says it cut data center water use by 25% from its 2022 baseline, introduced zero water cooling designs for new AI optimized facilities beginning in 2024, and replenished more water than it withdrew globally in fiscal year 2025. [Google](https://9to5google.com/2026/06/03/google-says-it-will-replenish-more-water-than-it-uses-at-data-centers-amid-public-pushback/?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com) says it replenished more than 7 billion gallons in 2025. It also shifted the first building at its Botetourt County, Virginia campus to air cooling after local pushback and has described a Texas site designed to use water primarily for kitchens. These changes are not merely public relations initiatives: they are practical responses to permitting, community trust, and local resource constraints. For systems where water is still required due to the extreme density of chips, new closed-loop water solutions are attempting to nearly eliminate water consumption.

## **Foreign Influence Driving Misinformation**

Researchers at[Alethea](https://info.alethea.com/research-state-actors-ai-slop-data-center-revolt?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com) identified roughly 700 references to U.S. data centers in Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state media over a six-month period. The content frequently connected AI infrastructure to water scarcity, higher electricity bills, environmental damage, and economic insecurity, seeking to turn legitimate local concerns into a broader indictment of the U.S. AI buildout. Chinese state outlets including[CGTN and the Global Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/09/business/china-russia-ai-data-centers.html?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com) amplified the claim that the AI boom was causing American electricity prices to rise, while Russian messaging portrayed local resistance as evidence that the industry was an unsustainable bubble.

The more troubling finding was the use of deceptive content intended to resemble local reporting or authentic grassroots activism.[Storm-1516](https://info.alethea.com/research-state-actors-ai-slop-data-center-revolt?utm_campaign=the-data-center-water-myth&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=konvoy.beehiiv.com), a Kremlin-linked influence operation, used fake domains designed to resemble TechCrunch and Gizmodo to distribute false claims about a data center in Armenia. Alethea also anonymously ran Facebook groups that presented themselves as local American communities, including pages with names such as “Life in Oklahoma” and “Only in Montana,” but were operated from Bangladesh and shared AI-generated anti-data-center material.

Water should not be used as a universal veto on AI infrastructure. It is one variable in a site-specific question, and one that should be assessed alongside power availability, land, cooling architecture, wastewater options, and permitting timelines. The winning operators of data centers will publish credible, site specific water metrics early, use lower water designs where conditions demand them, and distinguish real community concerns from claims that collapse under basic comparison against other use cases of water (i.e. agriculture, lawns, almonds, and golf courses).

**Takeaway:**The U.S. data center buildout will be constrained first by power, land, and permitting, not national water scarcity. Water still matters profoundly at the local level, but the public debate needs proportion and to be sensitive to our adversaries attempting to slow us down through misinformation campaigns (which have proven to be highly effective in the past). Lawns, almonds, and golf courses (just to name a few) are the much larger water users. The most durable data center projects will pair thoughtful cooling and water design with fast, transparent, evidence based community engagement.

Have a great weekend,

Josh
