Title: Graphic Designer ≠ Art Director ≠ Creative Director

URL Source: https://fatemaraja.substack.com/p/graphic-designer-art-director-creative

Published Time: 2026-09-16T12:30:57+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ynVR!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa348d672-4578-4fa1-87a7-4b3cb8fa6d0b_1536x1024.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ynVR!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa348d672-4578-4fa1-87a7-4b3cb8fa6d0b_1536x1024.png)

A few weeks ago I interviewed for an Art Director role.

Three rounds in, and finally a call with the founder and their head of marketing, but nobody was asking me how I’d run a shoot, or how I’d brief a set of freelance illustrators, or how I’d keep six different assets feeling like they came from the same brand. They were asking me what I thought the brand should stand for, whether I had a point of view on category positioning, and what “good” looked like across the whole business rather than just a single campaign.

I asked, plainly, who owned the creative vision there right now.

There was a pause, and then the founder said, half laughing, that this was honestly what they were hoping I would do.

I told them, as gently as I could, that what they’d just described wasn’t an Art Director. It was a Creative Director, and those are two different jobs with two different scopes, two different levels of accountability, and usually two very different salaries attached. The role on the job posting and the role in the room were simply not the same role.

They weren’t offended. If anything, they seemed relieved to have it named. Nobody on that founding team had a creative background. They’d written the job description off a template, borrowed a title that sounded senior enough, and never actually sat down to define what the work was. They knew they needed someone. They just didn’t know which someone.

I’ve now had a version of this conversation more times than I can count, with founders, with hiring managers, and honestly with designers themselves. Everyone’s using the same three job titles, and almost nobody agrees on what falls inside each one. The confusion isn’t really about industry, or seniority, or ego, even though it can look like all three. It’s that most people have never actually seen the boundaries drawn.

So here they are.

First, you’ve got founders and hiring managers who just don’t know the difference. They know they need someone senior and creative, so they slap a fancy title on the job post instead of actually sitting down and writing out what the job is. So you end up with a “Creative Director” listing that’s really an Art Director role, or an “Art Director” role that’s honestly just a Graphic Designer who’s also expected to hop on client calls. Nobody’s trying to trick anyone here, it’s just that most people running a business have never had to separate vision from direction from craft, because from where they’re sitting, all three look like the same thing: stuff that looks good.

And then on the other side, you’ve got designers inflating their own titles. Which, fair, “Director” just sounds better on an invoice than “Designer” does. And in small studios or freelance land, nobody’s really checking your credentials, you basically just... give yourself the title. Neither side is lying, exactly. Everyone’s just working off a job description that was never really accurate in the first place.

Honestly, what keeps me from getting annoyed at either side is this: the actual work, what a graphic designer does, what an art director does, what a creative director does, barely changes. Doesn’t matter if you’re at a five person startup, a two hundred person agency, a fashion house, or some tech company. What changes is just who’s doing it, how many people it’s split between, and what they end up calling it on the org chart. The work itself is basically the same everywhere. It’s only the staffing that’s different.

So let’s set the staffing stuff aside for a second and just walk through the three roles, starting with the one you can actually see and hold in your hands, then working up to the stuff that we call strategy.

The graphic designer is the person who actually makes the thing, which is what makes this role the easiest of the three to spot. You’re looking straight at the result.

They take a brief, a brand system, whatever instructions land on their desk, and turn it into something real: a layout, a social tile, a packaging file, a deck, a web page. Someone’s picking the point size on a headline, making sure a grid holds together so twelve different assets still look like they belong to the same family.

It’s more craft than concept. A brand’s voice only becomes real to a customer through small, repeated decisions, the same weight of type on every label, the same colour showing up consistently whether it’s on a screen, a shopfront, or a shipped box. Nobody’s reading your brand deck. They’re reading whatever a designer made from it, which means the designer is often the only part of the strategy anyone outside the company ever actually sees. Mess up that translation and it doesn’t matter how sharp the concept was, it never reaches anyone.

A designer’s answering “how do I make this well,” not “what should we even be making.” Designers usually aren’t the ones coming up with the idea, they’re bringing someone else’s idea to life, even though there’s real judgment happening here too, kerning, hierarchy, which headline actually reads better at a glance. A bad designer can tank a great concept just as easily as a great one can save a mediocre one. What they don’t usually own is the why. That’s one level up.

This looks different depending on where you are, but the job underneath stays the same: make the brand feel recognisable right at the point someone actually runs into it. In publishing, that’s laying out a feature story so it breathes across a spread. In consumer goods, it’s a label that reads the same across five SKUs. In tech, it’s UI screens inside a design system, so a product feels like one thing instead of screens built by different teams on different days.

Worth saying too, plenty of designers wear more than one of these hats on any given day, especially outside bigger companies. A senior designer at a small brand might fix kerning in the morning and basically art direct a shoot in the afternoon.

Which is why craft is never the lesser job here, whatever the org chart says. A brilliant idea still lives or dies in the hands of whoever’s actually making it, because a brand gets built one touchpoint at a time, in front of a real customer.

The art director decides how an idea should look and feel across every medium it touches, and makes sure everyone bringing it to life is working toward the same outcome.

The clearest way to draw this line is that a graphic designer is focused on executing the work, while an art director is focused on the concept behind it, meaning they’re less concerned with how one thing looks in isolation and more concerned with whether every visual choice across a project is in service of the same idea. Where a graphic designer is occupied with a single piece of visual communication, an art director is usually responsible for everything visual on a project at once, including video, illustration, motion, sound and photography alongside design. If a campaign needs a shoot, a set of illustrations, a typeface pairing, and a landing page to all feel like they came from the same brain, the art director is the one holding that thread.

This role works closely with a team of creative professionals, including designers, illustrators, photographers, and copywriters, defining the visual direction of a project, guiding the people executing it, and keeping the output aligned with the creative vision, while also translating what the client or business actually needs into a brief the creative team can act on.

This is also where the job starts to carry real stakes for the brand as a whole. An art director’s real value isn’t managing a roster of designers on an org chart, it’s making sure a customer can move from a billboard to a product shelf to an Instagram story and never once sense that three different teams made three different things. Cohesion is the actual product here. Done well, nobody notices it, a brand simply feels like itself everywhere it shows up. Done poorly, the brand starts to feel like six companies that happen to share a logo.

Again, this looks different by industry even though the job is the same. At a fashion brand, an art director might be the one on set deciding how a garment should be lit, styled, and photographed to match the story the collection is telling. At a food or beverage company, they’re directing how packaging, photography, in-store displays, and social content all read as one visual world. At an advertising agency, they’re the one turning a creative director’s campaign idea into an actual key visual, storyboard, or shoot. In publishing, they might be the one commissioning illustrators and photographers and deciding how a whole issue holds together visually.

Get the art direction right and a brand starts to feel inevitable, as though it could never have looked any other way. Get it wrong, and even a genuinely good idea starts to fray the moment it leaves the deck and meets the real world.

The creative director owns the why underneath everything the art director and designer are executing.

This is the leader of the creative department as a whole, responsible for bringing a project or brand’s creative vision to life, and unlike an art director, they typically supervise both the copywriters, brand marketers, and the designers, which means the scope isn’t just visual. It spans language, tone, strategy, and how the creative work ladders up to an actual business outcome. A creative director is in the room when a brand decides what story it’s telling this year, what a launch needs to feel like to hit its numbers, and which ideas get killed before they ever reach an art director’s desk.

This is the role most often confused with the other two, mainly because most creative directors came up through design or art direction and can still do that work with their eyes closed. But the job is different in kind, not just seniority. A creative director isn’t primarily judged on whether a layout is clean. They’re judged on whether the idea was right, whether the work actually differentiated the brand, and whether it moved the number it was meant to move.

Here’s where the scope tends to surprise people who’ve only worked in services or marketing. In industries with a physical product, a creative director’s influence usually reaches past the campaign and into the product itself. At a fashion house, the creative director isn’t just shaping the ad imagery around a collection, they’re shaping the collection, weighing in on silhouettes, fabrication, and which pieces even make it to production. At a beauty or fragrance company, the creative director might influence bottle design, packaging structure, or which scent concept gets greenlit, not just how it’s advertised. At a furniture or product design company, they can shape material choices and form language alongside the marketing that eventually sells it. In tech, the equivalent person, often carrying a title like Head of Design or Design Director, can shape the actual interaction language and visual tone of the product, not only the campaign that launches it. The common thread is that the creative director’s fingerprints show up anywhere the brand’s point of view gets expressed, and in physical product industries that point of view often extends into the object itself.

This is why the absence of a creative director rarely feels like a design problem. It feels like a strategy problem: a campaign calendar full of individually polished work that adds up to nothing, a team executing beautifully against a brief nobody actually wrote, a brand that photographs well but couldn’t tell you, in a single sentence, what it stands for. The creative director is the reason a business’s creative output is a point of view rather than a pile of assets.

This, by the way, is exactly the gap that founding team had left open. They wanted someone who could execute, which is what they thought they were hiring for. They had nobody who’d decided what the work was supposed to say in the first place.

Now that all three are on the table, it might help to watch them work together on something outside advertising entirely: lets take a gallery show.

Start with the graphic designer, the wall text has to be legible from four feet away without shouting for attention. The catalogue has to reproduce the artist’s actual palette rather than a rough approximation of it, which means understanding exactly how ink behaves on uncoated stock and how a colour that reads true under gallery lighting can shift the moment it’s printed on a page. The invitation has to signal the tone of an opening night in a single glance, before anyone has set foot inside. Almost none of this gets credited by name, and almost none of it is glamorous, but get it wrong and the whole show starts to feel amateurish the second someone can’t read a label or opens a catalogue where the colours bear no relation to what’s actually on the wall.

Above that sits the art director, who decided what those individual pieces should add up to. They set the sequence a visitor moves through: which piece greets you at the entrance, which one you’re meant to turn a corner and be surprised by, how the lighting falls differently on something meant to feel intimate versus something meant to overwhelm, how much white wall is left to breathe between pieces so the eye isn’t exhausted by the third room. The designer’s wall text and catalogue only do their job because the art director already decided the order in which they’d be encountered.

And above both of them is the creative director, the curator, who made the decisions nobody in the room will ever see credited by name. Long before anyone walked through the door, they decided which artist gets the show, whether it opens in the quiet of January or the charged energy of a spring art week when half the city is already looking, and which gallery actually suits the work: a cavernous industrial space for something monumental, an intimate townhouse room for something quieter and more confessional. They decided what the show is actually about, the argument running underneath it, the thread that should be visible from the first piece to the last. None of that shows up on a wall label as “creative direction.” It’s simply the decision that the sequencing, the labels, and the catalogue were all built to serve.

Three different people, three different skill sets, one show, and each one only makes sense in light of the one above it.

Here’s the part that took me the longest to actually internalise. These three categories of work exist at every company, in every category. What changes with size isn’t the work, it’s how many people it’s split across.

At the solo, freelance, or two-or-three-person founding stage, one person is quietly doing all three jobs at once. There’s no confusion here, because there’s no one else in the room to be confused. It’s only the moment that person tries to hire that the trouble starts, because vision, direction, and craft have been living inside one head for so long that the seams between them have never had to become visible, not even to the person doing the work. That founder had effectively been the creative director of their own company for two years without ever once needing the word.

At the small studio or growing startup stage, mismatched titles are most common, not out of dishonesty but because the company can only afford one senior creative hire and needs that person to be everything at once. The scope is often genuinely two or even three roles compressed into one, and the title, salary, and job description rarely reflect that accurately unless someone stops to name it.

At the mid-size agency or in-house team stage, this is usually the first point where the three roles separate into different humans. One creative director sets vision across a small roster, or a brand’s full output; one or two art directors each own a category or channel, and a bench of designers executes under them.

At the large agency or enterprise brand stage, the roles are fully specialised and fully separate. A chief creative officer or executive creative director sets vision across the whole brand or client roster, several creative directors each own a category, senior art directors run individual campaigns, and dozens of designers execute under them.

I want to be honest about where I land on this, because it would be easy to read the last few thousand words as an argument that titles matter enormously. To me, they don’t, not in themselves.

What I care about is scope, and whether the compensation on offer actually matches it. A title is just a label for a bundle of decisions someone is accountable for. If a company wants to pay me a designer’s rate, I want a designer’s scope, not a creative director’s ownership with a designer’s paycheck attached, which is a version of that founder’s mistake I’ve seen far more often than I’d like. And if I’m doing creative director-level work, setting the point of view, owning the outcome, being the person a business is actually relying on to get the why right, I want to be paid and credited like that’s what I’m doing, whether or not the business card says so.

That’s the actual use of this taxonomy. Not gatekeeping who gets to call themselves what, just being precise enough about the scope of the work- yours or the person’s you’re hiring, that nobody ends up over-titled and underpaid, or under-titled and quietly doing three jobs for one salary.

So Why Do Titles Matter At All, Then?

If the scope is what actually matters, you might reasonably ask why the label matters at all. Here’s where I’ve landed. Titles stop being vanity and start being useful the moment you’re working inside a cross-functional organisation, one where the people you’re coordinating with aren’t other designers.

Inside a design team, everyone can usually feel the difference between direction and execution without needing a title to tell them. But the second you’re in a room with product, marketing, sales, and leadership- people who have never had to learn where art direction ends and creative direction begins, the title becomes the fastest available signal for what decision rights this person has and what they should be looped in on.

That’s the only reason I’d defend having one at all, not because it captures what you actually do, but because it lets the rest of the organization know how to work with you without re explaining your job every time.

That founder and I didn’t finish the interview that day still talking about an Art Director role. We spent the rest of the call redrawing the job description from scratch, figuring out what they actually needed someone to own and what they were still going to have to figure out themselves before any hire, me or otherwise, could do it for them.

I don’t know yet if I’ll take the job, but I know exactly what job it would be if I did. Increasingly, that’s the only thing I actually care about knowing before I say yes.

👋 Hi, I am Fatema. I work with consumer brands on design, brand strategy and creative direction. In my weekly newsletter _[Layer by Layer](https://fatemaraja.substack.com/)_, I peel back the layers of brand, design, and culture. If this essay made you think differently about how brands are built, subscribe, and I will see you next week.

Title: Inside the creator economy’s AI reckoning

URL Source: https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning

Published Time: 2026-09-16T12:00:03+0000

Markdown Content:
Few phenomena within the creator economy have moved as fast as AI’s embrace. What was once treated with anxious suspicion is now more widely viewed as a necessary strategy.

Last year, according to [Kameron Buckner](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kameronmbuckner/), founder of [Social Docket](https://www.socialdocket.ai/), which helps creators navigate the legal implications of their work, the conversation around AI was defined by dread. This year, she says, the tone has shifted from fear to leverage — less “this thing is going to take over” and more how do we actually use it.

I spent the last several weeks talking to Buckner and others closest to this shift: top creators, consultants, founders, and social media strategists. Unsurprisingly, those who returned from the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity this year said AI was a centerpiece of the discourse.

But across the board, I sensed no real fear. Everyone I spoke to is using AI. Some more than others, some with discernment, others with keen enthusiasm. What’s certain is that AI has brought new questions to an industry built on areas like increasing productivity, monetizing creativity, and protecting IP. The bottom line: using it wisely is the difference between staying ahead of the curve and getting drowned out by it.

**Table of Contents**

*   [The Accelerator vs. The Author](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning#the-accelerator-vs-the-author)
*   [Legal is trying to catch up.](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning#legal-is-trying-to-catch-up)
*   [Does AI level the playing field, or widen the gap?](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning#does-ai-level-the-playing-field-or-widen-the-gap)
*   [The consensus: Humans remain irreplaceable.](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning#the-consensus-humans-remain-irreplaceable)

[](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning)
## The Accelerator vs. The Author

[DonYé Taylor](https://www.donyetaylor.com/) has been the mastermind behind culture-shifting campaigns and marketing strategies for brands like LVRN, Amazon, Nike, and Essence. She now runs her own functional-philosophy-meets-interior-design brand, Nuclei, alongside her newsletter, Mentally I’m Here. She believes AI doesn’t stand a chance against the ideas floating in her own brain — like one of her latest products, fittingly called the Brain Bank.

“AI is like a calculator,” says Taylor. “Just because I have a TI-89 doesn’t mean I’m going to get the right answer. I still need to put the right inputs into the calculator.”

[Alicia Richardson](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alicia-richardson/), head of community and brand partnerships at FiveTwoNine and the founder of Black Create Connect, shares this sentiment. “It can enhance your creativity,” she says. “It doesn’t _create_ your creativity. When it comes to raw, creator-led work specifically, she doesn’t think AI is ever going to take over, because audiences connect to people, not outputs.

Buckner tells her clients to think of AI less like a finished product and more like a running start. “Why start from a blank sheet of paper when you can start from an outline?” she says. In her own daily practice, prompting AI well has made her a better manager of actual human beings, because it forces her to get precise about what she wants before she asks for it. She applies that same instinct to her own visibility as a founder, using [HubSpot’s AEO tool](https://www.hubspot.com/products/aeo-lp?hubs_content=blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning&hubs_content-cta=hubspots-aeo-tool&hubs_post=blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning&hubs_post-cta=hubspots-aeo-tool) to check whether Social Docket shows up when someone searches for creator contract tools.

[Gigi Robinson](https://www.gigirobinson.com/), a content creator and founder of the social media consulting business Hosts of Influence, works with her team to feed 15-plus minutes of raw footage into AI video tools to get a rough cut before a human editor touches it. The software finds the “book-worthy” moments, but a person still decides what makes the final edit. The payoff shows up in her numbers, too: Robinson estimates AI saves her more than 10 hours a week and has driven a 20%-plus increase in her income.

Similarly, [Lindsey Gamble](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lindsey-gamble/), vice president of creator strategy & innovation at IZEA, highlights a productivity trend. Creators are building their own searchable content hubs, feeding years of newsletters and old captions into an AI tool to surface through-lines they’d otherwise forget they’d already covered.

No matter how efficient these tools become, Buckner emphasizes, they’re not replacing what actually makes someone worth hiring. “I don’t think any of these tools are going to substantially replace depth of knowledge and expertise,” she says.

[](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning)
## Legal is trying to catch up.

If AI hasn’t caught up to human expertise, the law hasn’t caught up to AI. “Law is so far behind, it’s never going to be able to catch up to the speed of technology,” says Buckner. “We’re still citing cases from like 1963.”

With many rules still unwritten, brands have started pushing the boundaries of what they can ask for. Buckner has started seeing a new kind of clause — brands willing to let creators use AI, on the condition that the creators hand over access to their prompts and processes. Her response is clear: “Immediately, no. That’s unnecessary access.”

In her view, the prompting process, not just the finished post or video, is where a creator’s actual thinking lives. Handing it over gives a brand insight into a creator’s mind that has nothing to do with the deliverable they paid for. Regardless of whether the law formally recognizes it yet, she suggests creators establish their own boundaries.

Gamble has seen the inverse version of this play out in creator contracts: brands banning AI use outright. One clause he recently encountered required that a creator not use any AI software, tools, or technologies without the brand’s prior written consent. He predicted that creators, not just brands, would eventually start writing their own AI-use clauses into agreements, protecting how their content and voice can be repurposed by brands using AI, not just the other way around.

[Annie-Mai Hodge, founder of Girl Power Marketing](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anniemaihodge/) (and also a HubSpot partner), sees a different platform-specific contradiction playing out. Social platforms are pushing AI tools directly into creators’ dashboards, she says, while simultaneously penalizing the content those same tools produce. “We are stuck in this incredibly frustrating paradox where platforms demand AI adoption but punish the output,” says Hodge. The result, she argues, is creators who are either too nervous to experiment with the tools they’re being handed, or too afraid to admit they already have.

Robinson has witnessed what happens when creators rely on AI without fully understanding the fine print. She points to a creator who partnered with one brand, then posted content for a direct competitor just two weeks later. That fell well within the exclusivity window most brand deals require — something Robinson knows firsthand from her own partnerships with the same agency.

She wonders, “Was that an AI problem that she didn’t actually read and comprehend, because she just sent it to AI and said, ‘negotiate for me’?”

On another note, the mere act of feeding a confidential contract into a public tool like ChatGPT, Robinson notes, can sometimes itself put a creator in breach, depending on how strict the brand’s legal team is.

This is precisely why Buckner is so passionate about the legal support she offers to creators. AI can help a creator understand what a term like “perpetuity” means, she says, but it can’t tell them how that term will actually play out in their specific circumstances. Connecting the definition to the real-life consequence, Buckner believes, is still a human job.

[](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning)
## Does AI level the playing field, or widen the gap?

In many ways, AI has become the great equalizer. Gamble sees that case play out constantly in his work with creators. What once required a big budget is now available to anyone with a laptop and a subscription. “It gives them the tools that bigger creators have with teams and dedicated staff and more funds,” he says of emerging creators. Scripts, captions, rough cuts, carousels — the entire production pipeline that once required hired help now takes minutes.

The same tools that lower the barrier to entry are also flattening what comes out the other side. “If everyone’s using the same thing and doing the same thing, a lot of the content feels the same,” Gamble says. It’s a byproduct of thousands of creators prompting the same handful of AI tools in largely the same ways.

According to [data from Lean In](https://leanin.org/report/women-in-the-workplace/) cited by Hodge, women are 22% less likely than men to be regular AI users at work, and 32% more likely to worry they’ll be seen as “cheating” if they use it. “While it’s my choice to keep AI out of my core workflow,” says Hodge, “we need to look at why women are conditioned to feel guilty for plugging it into their daily operations.”

Meanwhile, Hodge sees a different, more positive version of this play out in negotiations, where AI has actually started closing a different kind of gap around pay. Rate transparency has long been one of the creator economy’s biggest taboos, she says, and AI chatbots have made it easier for creators to find industry benchmarks. It might not get the brand to pay the creator more, but “it gives the creator more power and confidence to negotiate,” she adds.

[](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/creator-economy-ai-reckoning)
## The consensus: Humans remain irreplaceable.

If there was one word Robinson heard most at Cannes this year — even more than “AI” or “creators” — it was the word human. She reads it as a sign that even at a major marketing event, people still wanted to know a human was driving the work.

For Taylor, the answer is simple. “AI does not have feelings, it does not have emotion,” she says. “You can’t replace human connection.”

Gamble sees the cost of skipping that human step play out in real time, especially on LinkedIn. “Everyone’s writing sounds the same,” he says. “No one really has a voice, because everyone’s using the same thing.” His metaphor for what’s lost is that creativity is a muscle. The moment you stop using it, you lose it, the same way a body does when it stops training.

Gamble’s suggestion to creators is to protect that muscle, periodically writing, filming, or ideating without any tools at all, the way they did before AI existed. He also flags disclosure as a variable creators should watch closely — content that reads as AI-generated and undisclosed, he’s noticed, tends to get an immediate cold reception from audiences.

Richardson draws the same conclusion from the brand side. Raw, AI-generated animation has its place, she says, but when it comes to creator-led content specifically, she doesn’t see AI taking over. “People connect with human beings, and that won’t ever change.”

Hodge still reads every social media update herself each week, summarizing them in her own words, rather than automating the process. “Some people might think I’m mad for doing it that way,” she says, “but respectfully, ChatGPT and Claude can’t do it like I can.” Her advice to other creators: you don’t need to avoid the tools, you just need to be precise about where they belong. “If you are going to use it,” she says, “make it work harder for you.” In other words, it’ll never _be_ you.

Title: Perplexity Is Turning Creator Marketing Into a Product Test

URL Source: https://wersm.com/perplexity-turning-creator-marketing-into-product-test/

Published Time: 2026-09-16T12:02:45+00:00

Markdown Content:
Perplexity is treating creator marketing less like a sponsorship machine and more like a product demonstration team.

As [Digiday reports](https://digiday.com/marketing/perplexity-is-betting-big-on-creators/), the AI company recently advertised for a creator-marketing executive, although the listing is no longer accepting applications and Perplexity says the role was a backfill rather than a newly created function.

The brief still reveals where the company wants creator activity to go. The role covered campaigns involving more than 100 creators, multi-million-dollar budgets, deal negotiation and a direct relationship with growth marketing. The success metric was not simply reach. Perplexity wanted creator work tied to conversion.

That changes the job. Creators would not just explain why Perplexity is interesting. They would need to show what it can actually do, including reviewing original “builds” made with Perplexity Computer. The reported salary range was $175,000 to $225,000, suggesting the company sees this as a serious operating function rather than a loose influencer brief.

## The trust problem is part of the campaign

Perplexity says it works with hundreds of influencers, from niche creators to names such as Lewis Hamilton and Joe Rogan. But scale alone will not solve the harder problem: many creators see AI as a technology that could threaten parts of their livelihoods.

That makes creator marketing unusually exposed. A creator can make an AI tool feel practical and usable, but can also make the company’s outreach look like an attempt to recruit potential critics before the broader relationship has been worked out.

Digiday cites Ben Woods of Enders Analysis, who argues that the immediate goal is likely product adoption rather than an explicit campaign to repair AI’s image. That distinction matters. Perplexity is competing in a crowded market where users need a reason to choose one AI tool over another. Demonstrating a credible workflow may be more persuasive than asking creators to deliver broad brand approval.

The risk is that the demonstration becomes too polished. Creators will have to show genuine utility while acknowledging where AI changes the economics of creative work. For Perplexity, the strategic consequence is clear: creator partnerships are becoming a product test. If the tool cannot survive a creator’s real workflow, no amount of influencer reach will make the pitch credible.

Title: How much does a B2B content writer cost in 2026? — Lucy Jones Content Writer

URL Source: https://www.lucyjonescontentwriting.com/content-writing-blog/how-much-does-a-b2b-content-writer-cost-in-2026

Published Time: 2026-09-11T12:05:45+0100

Markdown Content:
This doesn’t really help you plan your budget, BUT I will do my best to shed some light on why this is a hard question to definitively answer.

## The short answer: 2026 B2B content rates

I’ve done some research (one of my fave things to do), and found some figures on how much freelance B2B content writers are changing in the UK in 2026:

### Per word

Per-word rates aren’t a popular way for freelancers to charge in 2026, to be honest. Expect to pay around the **30p to 50p per word** mark. Anything less than this is just too little to pay an experienced B2B content writer in 2026. Any cheaper, and the writer is likely a junior or is using AI to speed up the content creation process.

### Per hour

Some writers prefer to charge by hour, particularly if the client work required fluctuates a lot month to month. Expect to pay somewhere between **£50 and £100 per hour** for an experienced B2B content writer.

### Per article

This one varies wildly based on experience, word count and topic, but expect to pay between **£300 and £1,000** for a 1,000 to 3,000-word piece. At the £1,000 end, you’re probably looking at a long-form piece which requires extensive research, topic expertise, comfort with interpreting data and interviews.

### Day rate

Typically between **£350 and £800** for an experienced B2B content writer. The [ProCopywriters 2025 survey](https://www.procopywriters.co.uk/survey-2025/) puts the average day rate at £480, up 9% from the previous year.

### Case studies

Anywhere from **£400 to £1,000**, but expect it to cost **at least £600** if there is interviewing work involved.

### White papers

**£800 to as much as £4,000,**depending on length, topic and whether data analysis and interviewing are the responsibility of the freelancer.

### Web copy

**£250 to £600 per page, £350 to £800 for a conversion landing page**and **between £3,000 and £10,000 for a full small business website rewrite,**depending on how many pages the writer is producing and the topic expertise required.

### LinkedIn ghostwriting

Usually a monthly retainer, starting from around **£500**for a few posts, all the way up to **£3,000**for several posts per week. Expect to pay around **£100 per post on average**. However, B2B writers with lots of experience and topic specialisms may charge closer to **£250 per post**.

## The long answer

Now we’ve covered the rough numbers, let’s get into the details!

### What you’re really paying for

Per-word rates aren’t the desired way experienced B2B content writers want to be paid because all a word count does is tells you how long a piece is. It has nothing to do with how much work actually went into it. When I price up a project, I’m really pricing these things:

#### Research

A thin, _very_ lightly researched piece and a properly researched one might be the same length, but they don’t hold the same value. Not even close. Good research takes time, and that’s a big part of what you’re paying for.

#### Topic complexity

The more technical or regulated your industry, the more complex it is to write about it. The writer you hire needs to understand your industry and customers, which is why B2B tech, insurance and finance writers (like me) charge at the higher end.

#### SEO, GEO and AIO

On-page SEO is typically bundled in, but it isn’t free. Keyword research, structuring a piece to rank well and [show up in AI overviews and gen-AI tools](https://www.lucyjonescontentwriting.com/content-writing-blog/ai-is-changing-search-intent-and-heres-how) (GEO and AIO) takes expertise and time. If you want content that gets seen online, a writer with SEO experience is essential.

#### Interviews

You might want your writer to spend some time talking to your team or customers, but it will cost you (the content they create will be super valuable, though, so it’s absolutely worth the investment).

Your writer will need to arrange calls, prep for the chat, come up with suitable questions and write up the piece. It’s a lot of work, so expect to pay them well for it. If you choose the right B2B content writer, you won’t regret the end result!

#### Revisions

The writer you choose probably won’t get the piece exactly how you want it first time. If they do, you’ve either provided an incredible brief and freelancer onboarding process, or they’re a mind-reader.

Most writers will offer you several rounds of revisions to make sure the pieces they produce meet your expectations. Revisions take time, so if you expect the writer to offer several rounds of revisions because several stakeholders involved in the approvals process, expect to pay more.

### Freelance B2B content writer, agency or AI?

**Let’s say you’ve decided you want to publish four articles per month.** You’ve got some topic ideas and you’re ready to get moving. Now, you’ve got a choice to make: do you hire a freelance B2B content writer, a content agency, or use ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini? Let’s weigh up the pros and cons of each:

#### Freelance B2B content writer (∼cost: £800 to 1,600 per month)

**The pros:**

*   You work directly with the person writing the content. There’s no account manager passing information back and forth, which delays progress and creates opportunities for misunderstandings.

*   They get to know your business, your voice and your audience over time, so the content gets stronger while the briefing process gets much quicker.

*   They have experience writing for your sector, so they understand the buyers and the jargon from day one.

*   They’re flexible, allowing you to scale up work when you’re planning a big launch, and ease things off a little when things are quiet.

*   They’re much better value than an agency (because you’re paying for overheads) with the same or an even higher standard of writing, depending on the freelancer.

**The cons:**

*   Freelancers hit capacity. One person can only write so much, so availability might be limited and turnaround times might be longer than expected.

*   If they’re ill or go on holiday, there’s no team they can hand over to (and that’s why lots of us don’t go on holiday very often!).

*   Finding the right one takes a bit of effort. [I’ve got some advice about that](https://www.lucyjonescontentwriting.com/content-writing-blog/work-with-freelance-content-writer), if you’re interested.

#### Content agency (∼cost: £2,000 to £5,000 per month)

**The pros:**

*   They’ll have more capacity, and a big team means more content, regularity and cover when someone’s away.

*   Everything is under one roof: strategy, writing, editing, design and distribution, all managed for you.

*   It’s a good option if you’ve got a large, multi-format project to do, but very little time to manage it all.

**The cons:**

*   It will cost you. You’re paying for a big team and overheads, so the same content piece costs more than it would from a freelancer.

*   You might not deal with the individual writing the content directly. In agencies, account managers often manage the face-to-face with clients before passing information on to the writer. Vital details can get lost or misinterpreted.

*   There’s less flexibility, as agencies generally ask for minimum retainers and longer contracts than freelancers.

#### ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude (∼cost: £20 for a monthly subscription)

**The pros:**

*   It’s fast and cheap. You can have words in front of you in 15 seconds for a £20 per month subscription.

*   It might be useful for light research and content outlines.

**The cons:**

*   It can’t understand your customers, form real opinions or bring any first-hand experience to the content it produces. AI-generated B2B content feels flat, generic and lifeless. [B2B buyers still trust people over algorithms](https://www.affiliatesummit.com/blogs-1/b2b-buyers-still-trust-people-over-algorithms).

*   It gets things confidently wrong. In regulated fields, this can prove pretty disastrous.

*   Everyone is using the same tools, and that’s why everyone’s content is starting to sound the same. I like to call it “Claudification.”

*   AI content still needs human input for briefing and editing. A human writer needs to fact-check, edit and make it sound like its come from your business. People _really_[don’t like businesses churning out AI-generated content](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/harris-poll-ai-fatigue-less-trust-ai-generated-ads-cannes-lions).

### Here’s why the ‘cheap’ option ends up costing you the most

It’s tempting to see a £20 subscription and all the content you can generate as a big marketing win (although token limits do exist!). However, the content that comes out is just… bad. I’m always confused when I see people declaring they’ve outsourced much of their marketing to AI. It signals to me that they don’t have much (if any) marketing expertise. Weird way to admit you’re overconfident and don’t know what you’re doing.

This content still needs to be checked, corrected and (if you’ve got a B2B content expert around, who is probably horrified at what you’re doing) often needs to be completely rewritten. Generic content doesn’t rank well or impress potential buyers, so why create it? If you create enough of it, Google will mark you as creating spam content and punish you for it. Is it really worth the risk?

Then there’s the other risks to consider. In regulated fields like finance, insurance and health, missing a careless claim that an LLM generated can land you in compliance hot water. The risks are financial _and_ reputational.

## How much does a B2B content writer cost in 2026, really?

The honest answer to that question is that it depends on the level of writer expertise, the format and what you need the writing to do. If you’re looking for someone to genuinely understand your business and customers, create high-quality content quickly that ranks and shows up in AI tools, work with a B2B writer with expertise in your sector on a retainer. After a few months, they’ll know your business inside out and be able to create the content that helps you meet your marketing goals.

**_That’s my cue!_**I’m Lucy, a freelance B2B content writer with seven years experience and more than 1,500 pieces behind me, including long-form articles, case studies, white papers and web and social copy. I write for B2B brands and agencies across tech, SaaS, HR and recruitment, insurance and finance, and it’s my job to differentiate you online.

My content philosophy is research-led, human writing that ranks on Google because it brings something new and valuable to industry conversations, not more of the same. No boring, templated content playbooks here. I’m all about creating content that gets you seen online.

**Want to know how much it would cost to work with a B2B content writer like me?**[**Fill in my quick discovery questionnaire**](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdkAGLGSzN-DaEYB6ppH4ZaPow8OvLYiql5zPj2w6qfHb5Udw/viewform?usp=dialog)**and I’ll get back to you with a quote.**

Title: Economists Concerned the AI Bubble Is About to Blow

URL Source: https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/economists-late-stage-ai-bubble-federal-reserve-inflation

Published Time: 2026-09-16T13:46:05-04:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: A photo shows a bubble bursting.](https://futurism.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/economists-late-stage-ai-bubble-federal-reserve-inflation_af90e4.jpg?quality=85&w=1152)

 Getty Images / Xvision 

With Wall Street on pins and needles amidst a wide-ranging discussion of AI safety, we may well be living through one of the most consequential weeks for the future of AI in the United States.

That doesn’t necessarily mean we’re headed to an ascendant future for the AI industry. According to London-based firm Capital Economics, the entire economy of the Western world is currently mired in a “late-stage bubble” — a massive misallocation of capital fueling the AI boom, [_Fortune_ reported](https://fortune.com/2026/09/14/is-ai-stock-market-bubble-federal-reserve-interest-rates/).

In a recent analysis, also flagged [by _Fortune_](https://fortune.com/2026/09/13/stock-market-outlook-late-stage-bubble-crash-2027-treasury-yields-5-percent/), Capital Economics senior markets economist James Reilly surveyed eight types of market indicators, finding the vast majority at or near critical levels. These indicators amount to blinking warning lights on the economic dashboard, which have historically only lit up ahead of massive fall-offs in market euphoria: equity and debt issuance is surging, market-cap is concentrated in just a few massive tech stocks, and expected income growth for major indices is looking increasingly unstable.

Breaking down all that marketspeak is beside the point. The fact is, financial markets are under tremendous strain from the AI buildout, and the only precedent for this moment comes from the months before markets crash, like the peak of the dot-com boom.

“On balance, we think the data look consistent with a late-stage bubble,” Reilly wrote in his analysis. “Most of the factors we consider are at, or close to, levels that have preceded past stock market peaks.”

And as economists work to make sense of the precarious moment we’re in, the US Federal Reserve faces a critical decision: whether to apply the emergency brake, or sit back and pray the current market euphoria doesn’t drive us off a cliff.

Later this afternoon, Fed chair Kevin Warsh is [expected to announce](https://apnews.com/article/federal-reserve-warsh-trump-inflation-bab1bcb07e973bfb2dd0c3e5fbbb73b1) he’s raising interest rates, applying brakes that would make borrowing more expensive, and — in an ideal scenario — curb both [consumer and business spending](https://ramp.com/leading-indicators/the-warsh-case-scenario), thus cool inflation. Yet for as routine an exercise as that is, some say inflation isn’t the issue it’s being made out to be, arguing that Fed intervention in this moment would be without historical precedent.

As _Fortune_ reports, core [consumer price index](https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/core-inflation-rate) (CPI) inflation — a measure that excludes volatile costs like food and energy — reached a new post-pandemic low in August. That being the case, the analytics firm UBS expects the Fed to simultaneously lower its long-term inflation projections while raising interest rates anyway, something the company says has never happened before.

“That is really, really odd, indeed unique,” a UBS analyst wrote, quoted by _Fortune_.

Whatever the justification for that decision, its impact on the AI bubble will be telling. A [_CNN_ analysis](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/14/economy/federal-reserve-ai-inflation-rate-hike) notes there’s an acute possibility that rate hikes cool everything except runaway AI investments — in which case the warning lights could continue to blink as the brakes come all the way off.
